t.glovers reef marine reserve@16.8,-87.8:
Glover's Reef lies some fifty kilometres off the coast of Belize, a ring of coral enclosing a lagoon of turquoise water dotted with patch reefs, with a handful of small sandy cayes on its rim. It is one of only a few true atolls in the Caribbean, named after a pirate, John Glover, who is said to have used it as a base in the eighteenth century. Part of the Belize Barrier Reef Reserve System listed by UNESCO, it is a marine reserve where fishing is controlled, and its waters are home to sharks, rays, turtles, groupers and an extraordinary variety of corals and fish.

The cayes are tiny, with palm trees, a few cabins and research stations, and nothing else. Visitors come for diving, snorkelling, kayaking and fishing, and to enjoy the feeling of being at the edge of the world. The wall dives on the outer edge of the reef, where the coral drops into the deep blue, are famous among divers. There are no roads, of course, and no vehicles; the only way to get there is by boat, usually from Dangriga, Hopkins or Sittee River on the mainland, a journey of a couple of hours across sometimes choppy seas.

So your bike stays on the mainland, and the good news is that Belize has some excellent riding. The Hummingbird Highway, running from Belmopan to Dangriga, is one of the most scenic roads in Central America, winding through the Maya Mountains with jungle-covered hills, rivers and citrus plantations, and it is paved and well-maintained. The Southern Highway continues to Punta Gorda through villages and forest. Watch for speed bumps, cyclists, dogs and sudden tropical downpours, and avoid riding at night. The rainy season, roughly June to November, brings heavy rain and the risk of hurricanes.

Dangriga is the main town on the coast, with fuel, shops and restaurants; it is also the heart of the Garifuna culture, with its music, drumming and food, such as hudut, a fish and coconut stew with mashed plantain. Belizean food also includes rice and beans, stew chicken and fresh seafood. Leave your bike in a secure place before taking the boat, and pack light. Out on the reef, put on a mask, float above the coral and watch the fish; after days on the road, it is a different kind of freedom.
t.south water caye marine reserve@16.7,-88:
You cannot ride to South Water Caye, and that is rather the point. The reserve covers a stretch of the Belize Barrier Reef some twenty kilometres off the coast, with tiny islands of sand and palm, mangrove cays, turquoise shallows and the deep blue drop beyond the reef crest. It is one of the seven protected areas inscribed in 1996 as the Belize Barrier Reef Reserve System, part of the longest barrier reef in the Western Hemisphere.

Under the water there are coral gardens, sponges, rays, turtles, nurse sharks and, in the seagrass beds, the occasional manatee. On the islands, frigatebirds and boobies wheel overhead. Carrie Bow Caye, inside the reserve, hosts a long-running Smithsonian marine research station, and Tobacco Caye, a speck of land with a few guesthouses, is a popular base for snorkelling straight off the beach.

The bike stays on the mainland, in Dangriga, the main town of the Stann Creek district. Dangriga is the cultural heart of the Garifuna people, descendants of West African and Caribbean Indigenous peoples who arrived on this coast in the early nineteenth century. Garifuna Settlement Day on 19 November is celebrated with drums, dancing and re-enactments of the landings, and the town's music, punta, and food, such as hudut, fish cooked in coconut milk with mashed plantain, are worth seeking out. Boats to the cays leave from the town and from the nearby coast, depending on the weather.

Getting to Dangriga is one of the best rides in Belize. The Hummingbird Highway runs from Belmopan through the Maya Mountains, past citrus plantations, limestone hills, caves and river crossings, and is paved and winding, with a few narrow bridges. Rain can be sudden and heavy, especially from June to November, which is also hurricane season. The coastal roads south towards Hopkins and Placencia are flatter and sandier.

Dangriga has fuel, shops and simple restaurants. Bring sun protection, plenty of water and a dry bag for the boat ride, and remember that the reef is fragile: no touching corals, and reef-safe sun cream if you have it. Spending a night on one of the cays, with the generator off and the stars out, is a fine way to forget about tyres and chains for a while.
t.the village of olgino@60.0,30.1:
On the northern shore of the Gulf of Finland, just beyond the city's edge, Olgino is a place of pines, sand and low wooden houses, a seaside suburb that grew up a century and more ago as a retreat for Saint Petersburg families who wanted fresh air and the beach without travelling far. It is part of the World Heritage Site that wraps the historic city and its surroundings, which includes not only palaces but villages, parks and landscapes like this one.

The skyline here has changed dramatically. A couple of kilometres east, the Lakhta Center, a tapering glass tower more than 460 metres high and the tallest building in Europe, rises out of the flat shore like a needle. From the beach at Olgino it dominates every view, a sharp modern contrast to the low wooden datchas behind the dunes.

Follow the coast road west and you enter what was, before 1940, Finland. The Karelian Isthmus coast is lined with old resort villages: Sestroretsk, Komarovo and Repino, where the painter Ilya Repin lived and worked at his estate, the Penates, now a museum. The road runs through pine woods with glimpses of the sea and the occasional lake, and in summer the beaches are full of families.

The Primorskoye highway is busy on summer weekends, with long jams heading out of the city on Friday evening and back on Sunday. Elsewhere the riding is easy and flat, with sandy verges, pedestrians crossing to the beach and the odd speed camera. Winter turns the gulf into a white plain where people fish through holes in the ice.

Practical matters start with the big one: Russia is currently very difficult for most Western travellers, with sanctions and visa, insurance and payment obstacles, and many governments advise against going. If you are here, Lakhtinskiy, two kilometres away, has fuel and shops. Smoked fish from the gulf, especially the small smelt-like koryushka that Saint Petersburg celebrates each spring, is the local treat.
t.half moon caye natural monument@17.2,-87:
Half Moon Caye is a crescent of white sand and coconut palms on the edge of Lighthouse Reef, the most remote of Belize's three atolls, some eighty kilometres out into the Caribbean, and the one honest thing to say first is that you cannot ride there. The bike stays on the mainland, and you go out by boat for a long day trip or a few nights of diving.

The island is protected as a natural monument, the first in Belize, and it exists mainly for the birds. Its western half is covered in littoral forest where a colony of red-footed boobies nests in the trees, alongside magnificent frigatebirds, which steal food from the boobies in mid-air. A viewing platform lets you look out at eye level across the canopy full of nesting birds. On the ground, iguanas and lizards bask, and sea turtles come ashore to lay their eggs on the beaches. An old lighthouse stands on the eastern end, a reminder of the many ships that came to grief on the reefs here.

Underwater, the atoll is famous. The Great Blue Hole, a perfectly round marine sinkhole over three hundred metres across and more than a hundred metres deep, lies in the middle of the lagoon and was made famous by Jacques Cousteau, and the wall dives along the edge of the reef near Half Moon Caye drop away into deep blue water, with turtles, rays, reef sharks and big schools of fish. Snorkelling in the shallows is excellent, too. All of this is part of the Belize Barrier Reef Reserve System, listed by UNESCO in 1996.

On the mainland, riding in Belize has its own pleasures. The Hummingbird Highway, from Belmopan toward Dangriga, is the country's favourite ride, a winding road through citrus groves and jungle-covered limestone hills, with cave systems, rivers and swimming holes along the way. The Western Highway to San Ignacio and the Maya ruins is straighter and busier. Watch for speed bumps in every village and for unpredictable driving.

Trips to the atoll leave from Belize City and the cayes, usually very early in the morning, and the crossing can be rough when the trade winds blow, so a calm-weather day is worth waiting for. Bring sun protection and water, and leave nothing behind on the island. Fuel, food and secure parking for the bike are best arranged in Belize City or wherever you start the boat trip.
t.sestroretsky razliv@60.1,30.0:
Sestroretsk is a small town on the north shore of the Gulf of Finland, in a landscape of pine-covered dunes, shallow bays and lakes, and it has an industrial origin that surprises visitors. In 1721 Peter the Great founded an arms factory on the Sestra river here, and a dam created a broad reservoir to power it. That reservoir, Razliv, which means flood or spill, is the lake that gives the place its name. The water, ringed by reeds and birches, is a favourite spot for locals to swim, fish and walk.

Razliv has another claim to fame in Russian history. In the summer of 1917, when the Provisional Government was hunting for Vladimir Lenin, he hid in a hay shed and then a hut by the lake, disguised and in the company of a loyal worker, planning the revolution from there. The hut and a memorial are now a museum, set among trees on the shore, and the story is retold with great pride in Soviet-era guidebooks. Whatever you think of the politics, the setting is tranquil, and the idea of a revolution plotted in a hay shed has a certain absurd romance.

Riding along the north shore is relaxing. The roads run through pine forest and past dachas, with gentle bends and good surfaces, and in summer the beaches at Sestroretsk are crowded with sunbathers. The coast road offers views of the gulf and the hazy outline of Kronstadt, and the wind off the water keeps the air fresh. Traffic builds on summer weekends as city dwellers head for the seaside, so avoid late afternoon on Fridays and Sundays. The best months are June to September, and the winter roads can be icy.

Sestroretsk has fuel stations, shops, cafés and a long promenade, and Tarkhovka and Razliv have smaller services. Try smoked fish from the gulf or a bowl of fish soup called ukha, and a glass of kvass, a mildly fermented bread drink sold from tanks in summer. Walk along the shore at sunset, when the light is long and gold, and the dunes and pines glow.
t.blue hole natural monument@17.3,-87.5:
Be clear about one thing first: you cannot ride to the Great Blue Hole. It lies out in the Caribbean, about seventy kilometres off the coast of Belize, in the middle of Lighthouse Reef, and the only ways to reach it are a small boat on a long day trip or a sightseeing flight from Belize City. The bike stays on the mainland, which is perfectly good riding country, and the Hole is the excursion you take once you have settled in.

What you are looking for is a perfect circle of dark blue, about three hundred metres across, surrounded by the pale turquoise of the shallow reef, which is why it stands out so strongly from the air. It is a sinkhole, a limestone cave that collapsed at the end of the last ice age, when sea levels were far lower, and then flooded as the water rose, and it plunges to something over a hundred metres. Jacques Cousteau brought his ship Calypso here in 1971 and declared it one of the top diving sites in the world, and divers still go down to the ledges to see stalactites formed when the cave was dry, and reef sharks cruising the gloom.

The Hole is part of the Belize Barrier Reef Reserve System, a World Heritage Site, and the whole region is a marine reserve, so look and do not touch. Nearby Half Moon Caye holds a colony of red-footed boobies, with a sandy beach and a lighthouse, and the water around it is clear enough for snorkelling.

For the ride, the useful base is Belize City, which has fuel and every service, or one of the coastal towns, and the Philip Goldson Highway runs inland across flat country of pine, cane fields and rivers, with speed bumps in every village and a fair amount of trucks. Belize is small, English is widely spoken and distances are short, so a loop to the Maya sites and back is easy. The dry season, from February to May, brings the calmest seas and the best visibility, while hurricanes can strike between June and November. Book the boat in advance, take sunscreen and a hat, and expect to be tired, salty and very happy.
t.laughing bird caye national park@16.4,-8:
Laughing Bird Caye is a tiny island, a sandy speck with a few palms, sitting on a barrier reef about sixteen kilometres off the coast of southern Belize, and it was named for the laughing gulls that once nested in huge numbers. The birds, whose call really does sound like a cackle, are mostly gone, driven off by hurricanes and people, though the name stuck. The island itself has shrunk, too. Hurricane Iris, in 2001, washed away much of the sand and the old palms, and since then conservation groups have worked to protect what remains.

The reef around it is the point, and it forms part of the Belize Barrier Reef system, which UNESCO listed in 1996, and later added the nearby Sapodilla Cayes. Snorkellers drift over colourful coral gardens, with parrotfish, rays and turtles, while divers go further out to the walls. Each spring, around the full moon from March to June, whale sharks gather at Gladden Spit, off the coast, one of the great wildlife sights of the Caribbean.

You reach the caye by boat from Placencia, a village at the end of a long, narrow peninsula between the lagoon and the sea. A paved road runs down the peninsula for about thirty kilometres, flat and straight, with palms, small hotels and the odd dog. Placencia itself, a village of around four thousand, has fuel, restaurants and boat operators, and the beach is a long strip of pale sand. The road to it leaves the Southern Highway, which is paved and fairly empty, but has speed bumps at every village and potholes after rain. This is easy riding, not demanding, though trucks hauling citrus and bananas use the highway.

The dry season, February to May, is best for calm water and clear days. June to November is the wet season, with heavy showers, strong winds and hurricane risk. Bring reef-safe sunscreen, a rash vest and cash, since boats and restaurants often prefer it. Eat fresh fish and lobster in season, which closes in summer, and finish with rum punch and a sunset over the lagoon, because every ride deserves a decent ending.
t.the park nearest dubki@60.0,30.0:
These coordinates fall on the north shore of the Gulf of Finland, near Lisiy Nos, the Fox's Nose, a suburb of Saint Petersburg where pine woods run down to the beach and the water is shallow and grey for a long way out. I cannot place a park called Nearest Dubki exactly, and I would rather say so than invent it. Dubki simply means little oaks, a common name for a patch of woodland, and the ride titles connect this spot with the Oranienbaum Springboard, which is the south shore, across the water, where a Soviet bridgehead held out through the siege of Leningrad from 1941 to 1944 while the city itself was encircled.

The north shore has its own character. It is a coast of sand, reed beds and pines, with a long cycle path, small ports and, a few kilometres east, the huge glass tower of the Lakhta Center, which rose in 2019 as the tallest building in Europe. The contrast between the old coast and that spike on the horizon is hard to miss. In winter the shallows freeze and people walk or ski far out on the ice, and in the white nights of June the sun barely goes down.

Riding here is easy but not exciting. The main road along the coast, the Primorskoe highway, is a busy trunk, and the side roads through Lisiy Nos and Lakhtinskiy are short, suburban and patched. Watch for tram lines and potholes, which are worst in spring after the frost. Early mornings are calm and the light over the water is soft, and autumn is the best season, with clean air and golden birch.

Lisiy Nos has fewer than five thousand people, so fuel is not guaranteed in its small streets, but the city's petrol stations are close, and Lakhtinskiy has more services. Expect to find coffee kiosks and small cafes near the beach in summer. If you plan to travel in the region, check the rules on entry and on bringing a vehicle in advance, as they have changed recently and I cannot say what applies today.
Where the Neva leaves Lake Ladoga there is a small island in the current, and for seven centuries whoever held it controlled the river and the trade route to the Baltic. The Novgorodians built the first wooden fort here in 1323 and called it Oreshek, the Little Nut, because of the island's shape. The Swedes took it in 1611 and renamed it Nöteborg, and in 1702 Peter the Great stormed it, and renamed it Schlüsselburg, the Key Fortress. The old stone walls and towers stand now on a low island reached by a short boat ride from the town, which is now called Shlisselburg.

Over the following centuries the fortress became a prison for political enemies of the tsars. Decembrists were held here, and in 1887 Alexander Ulyanov, Lenin's older brother, was executed within its walls for his part in a plot against the tsar. In September 1941 the Germans took the town and cut Leningrad's last land link, yet the small Soviet garrison on the island fortress is remembered for holding out, and the siege was first broken in January 1943 on this very stretch of the Neva. It is a battered, quiet place today, and the red brick under the grey sky has a bleak, honest beauty.

The ride here is a long, flat run east from Saint Petersburg along the Neva, across country of birch, pine and bog, with small settlements and the odd industrial town. The road is busy on weekends but has a decent surface, and the river appears now and then through the trees, broad and slow. In summer the light holds until late, and boats cross to the island regularly. In winter the ice on the river changes everything and the island becomes a stage set.

Shlisselburg has about twelve thousand people and has fuel, shops and cafes, as does the neighbouring Imeni Morozova. Allow an hour or two for the island, and bring a windproof layer, because the river wind is sharp. As elsewhere in Russia, the rules for foreign visitors and vehicles are not what they were, so check before you plan. The Neva view from the pier is the best part of the trip.
t.kronstadtsky@60.0,30.0:
This stretch is the north shore of the Gulf of Finland, the coast that runs west from the Neva delta toward Sestroretsk and the Karelian Isthmus. The label points to the Kronstadtsky district name rather than a single monument, so think of it as a tract of seaside land, with the port town of Lisiy Nos about five kilometres away and the larger suburb of Lakhtinsky eight kilometres off. Lisiy Nos means Fox's Nose, a cape that pokes out into the gulf, and from here on a clear day you can look south across the water to the low silhouette of Kotlin Island.

The country is flat, sandy and pine-covered, with drifts of reeds along the shore and dunes in places. It is a landscape of dachas, where Petersburgers have gone to escape the heat for over a century, and the roads between them are narrow, sometimes sandy at the edges, and lined with wooden fences and gardens. In summer the smell is resin, damp grass and barbecue smoke. Speeds are low and the corners are tight little turns around gardens and drainage ditches, not real riding country, but pleasant to wander through at an unhurried pace.

The history here is bound up with the defence of the city. Finland's border lay terribly close to St Petersburg until the Second World War, and these shores saw fortifications, patrols and, later, long periods of restricted access. Some of the old military structures still stand among the pines. Today the area is mostly leisure: walkers on the shoreline, cyclists on the paths, and anglers at the water's edge in early morning.

For practical matters, Lakhtinsky and its neighbours have fuel and shops, and the main road into the city is only a few kilometres south. The best time to come is a bright morning in late May or June, when the pines are warm and the gulf is calm, or on a September weekday when the crowds have thinned. Do not expect much in the way of views from the road itself; the water is hidden behind trees most of the time.
t.willi willi np@-31.1,152.4:
The coast of northern New South Wales is famous for beaches, but a few hours inland the land climbs into a different world of ridges, gorges and old rainforest. Willi Willi National Park lies in the hills behind Kempsey and Port Macquarie, in country that belongs to the Dunghutti people, and it protects a patch of that wilder landscape. The region is part of the broad belt of rainforest and wet eucalypt forest that runs up the Great Dividing Range, the remnants of an ancient forest that once covered the supercontinent of Gondwana.

What you find here depends on the elevation. Lower slopes have tall eucalypts, blackbutt and flooded gum, with ferns and vines underneath. Higher up, the forest becomes cooler and wetter, with giant tree ferns, moss-covered trunks and strangler figs. Wildlife is secretive but varied: koalas, quolls, gliders, wallabies, lyrebirds and an enormous number of frogs after rain. Leeches are a fact of life in wet weather, and the humid smell of leaf litter after a storm is unforgettable. There are also limestone caves in the area that give the park its fame among cavers.

Riding here is a mixture of sealed roads and gravel. The main roads from Kempsey climb into the hills with long curves, but the park's own roads can be rough, and heavy rain can wash out sections or close them. Check with the national parks service before you go. Mist and low cloud are common, so visibility can drop quickly, and wet leaves on the road are as slippery as ice. Logging trucks use some of the tracks, and kangaroos and wallabies come out at dusk, so avoid riding after dark.

There are no sizeable towns near the park, so fill the tank in Kempsey or Wauchope before you head up, and carry water and food. Small villages in the foothills sometimes have a general store, but hours are short. Autumn and spring are the best seasons, when the weather is mild and the roads are mostly dry. Summer can be hot and stormy, and winter nights can be cold at altitude. In the early morning the sound of birds is overwhelming, and the light through the canopy is green and gold.
t.historic centre of saint petersburg@60.0:
Stand on Palace Square at midday and you are in the staging area of two centuries of Russian history. The great curved yellow General Staff building wraps one side, the green and white Winter Palace fills another, and in the middle rises a granite column topped by an angel. The palace was designed in the 1750s by Bartolomeo Rastrelli for Empress Elizabeth, in a flamboyant Baroque that makes every other palace in Europe look restrained, and it was from here that the Russian emperors ruled until 1917. Today it holds the Hermitage, one of the world's biggest art museums, whose collection began with Catherine the Great's purchases and now fills several buildings along the Neva.

The historic centre of Saint Petersburg, listed by UNESCO in 1990, is a planned city, and that is its charm. Streets are straight, with long perspectives ending in spires, and canals curve through it in careful arcs. Nevsky Prospect runs in a dead straight line from the Admiralty with its golden needle, past the Kazan Cathedral with its curved colonnade, to the Alexander Nevsky Monastery. On the other side of the Neva stands the Peter and Paul Fortress, where the emperors are buried, and the Church of the Saviour on Spilled Blood, a many-coloured fantasy of onion domes built where Alexander II was assassinated in 1881.

The city has a tragic chapter, too. During the siege of Leningrad, from September 1941 to January 1944, around nine hundred days, hundreds of thousands of residents died, mostly of starvation, while the city refused to surrender. Memorials and cemeteries recall it.

Riding in the centre is not recommended: traffic is heavy, trams rule the roads and parking is almost impossible. Leave the bike somewhere secure and walk. Fuel and services are everywhere in the wider city, which has over five million inhabitants. Be aware that travel to Russia by foreign motorists is currently heavily restricted, and the situation changes quickly.

Visit in the white nights of June if you like light, or in the cold clarity of winter for fewer crowds. In every season, take comfortable shoes, because distances here are bigger than they look. In the old cafes, order a pastry called pyshka, a sugared doughnut, and tea from a samovar.
t.sortavala@61.7,30.7:
Sortavala is a Finnish town that happens to be in Russia. It stands at the head of a long bay on the northern shore of Lake Ladoga, in the Republic of Karelia, among granite ridges, pine woods and hundreds of small islands, and until 1940 it was part of Finland, known by the name Sortavala as well. The territory passed to the Soviet Union after the Winter War and the Continuation War, and most Finnish residents were evacuated. The architecture they left, including the town hall, the old seminary and several stone buildings in the National Romantic style, gives the centre a look quite unlike any Russian town.

Ladoga is Europe's largest lake, almost a sea, and in the archipelago near Sortavala the water is clear, dark and cold, with bare rock islands and ferry boats. Boats leave from here to the island monastery of Valaam, one of the most important Orthodox sites in northern Russia. Inland, about twenty kilometres away, the marble quarry at Ruskeala has flooded into a turquoise lake, and its stone was used in Saint Petersburg's grand buildings. Karelia is also the landscape of the Kalevala, the Finnish national epic, which was collected from rune singers in these villages.

The A-121 highway, which runs north from Saint Petersburg along the western side of Ladoga, is the usual route, a long road through forests and past lakes with moderate traffic and a few lorries. Surfaces vary, with some smooth stretches and some patched and rutted sections, and wildlife such as elk can appear at dusk, so watch for it. Summer is bright with endless white nights, early autumn brings colour and mushrooming families, and winter is long, snowy and icy.

Because of the current political situation, travel to Russia is heavily restricted for many nationalities, and entry rules, insurance and border conditions change often, so check official advice before planning anything here. For practical matters, Sortavala has fuel, shops and cafes, and Khelyulya, a smaller settlement nearby, has basic services. Try kalitki, small open Karelian pies filled with potato or millet, and fish from the lake, usually smoked or served in a rich soup.
t.fenwicks scrub flora reserve@-31.3,152.1:
Werrikimbe National Park lies on the rim of the Great Escarpment in northern New South Wales, about a hundred kilometres inland from Port Macquarie, and it belongs to the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, a World Heritage area that preserves remnants of the forests that covered the ancient supercontinent. The landscape is high and wet, a plateau of eucalypt forest, tree ferns, swamp and cliffs where rivers begin their descent to the coast. Fenwicks Scrub is a small patch of this vegetation, a pocket of rainforest in the folds of the hills.

What is special here is the plant life. Antarctic beech, a southern hemisphere relative of the beeches that grow in Patagonia and New Zealand, survives in cool, misty gullies, and its twisted, moss-covered trunks look like something from a fairy tale. Ferns, orchids and lichens thrive. Animals include lyrebirds, whose calls imitate other birds and sometimes machinery, and wallabies, possums and quolls. Visitors also find leeches after rain, so wear long socks.

Getting here takes a bit of work. The roads leading into the park are largely unsealed forest tracks, with gravel, corrugations and creek crossings, and conditions vary with the weather. After heavy rain they can turn to slippery mud or wash out entirely, so check with the national park authorities before setting off. A sturdy adventure bike and sensible tyres make a big difference. Mobile coverage is poor to nonexistent, so tell someone your plans and carry a map. The cooler months, from autumn to spring, can see frost and fog, while summer thunderstorms are fierce.

Camping is possible at designated sites, with basic facilities, and you must carry water and supplies. The reward is silence broken only by birdsong and the drip of water from the leaves. Travel light and leave nothing behind.
t.petrozavodsk@61.8,34.3:
Peter the Great founded Petrozavodsk in 1703 as a foundry, a place to cast cannon for the war against Sweden, and the name means exactly that, Peter's works. The city has since grown into the capital of the Republic of Karelia, with about a quarter of a million people, and sits on the western shore of Lake Onega, the second largest lake in Europe after Ladoga. The long embankment along the water is the city's best feature, lined with modern sculptures that were donated by twin towns around the world, and in good weather the whole town seems to walk along it.

Onega is more like a sea than a lake. In summer the water is clear and cold, with rocky islets and long horizons, while in winter it freezes into a white plain and the shore shifts with ice. Hydrofoils run in season to Kizhi island, where the astonishing wooden churches stand, including the Transfiguration Church with its twenty-two domes, built without nails according to local tradition. The Kivach waterfall, one of the largest lowland waterfalls in Europe, lies north of the city and is a natural stop on the way to the interior.

The ride along the lake toward Sortavala, on the shore of Lake Ladoga, is a classic north European one. Roads cross low glacial ridges, pine and spruce forests and many small lakes, with granite rock coming through the soil, and the surface is mostly good with some patched sections. The landscape resembles neighbouring Finland, and indeed Karelia was disputed between Finland and Russia and changed hands during the twentieth century, a history written in place names and in abandoned Finnish houses. Traffic is lighter than around Moscow or St Petersburg, though trucks and tour buses slow things in summer.

Petrozavodsk has everything a rider needs, from fuel to repair shops, markets and restaurants serving local fish such as vendace and whitefish, along with the rye-crusted pies called kalitki that are a Karelian tradition. White nights in June make for very long riding days, while the warm months stretch from June to August. Mosquitoes and horseflies can be vicious in July, and autumn colours arrive in September, ahead of an early and hard winter.
t.sydney@-33.9,151.2:
Sydney's harbour is the reason it exists. The First Fleet arrived in 1788 and chose the sheltered cove where the city stands, on land long cared for by the Gadigal people of the Eora nation. The Harbour Bridge, opened in 1932 and known to everyone as the coathanger, and the Opera House, whose white sails by the Danish architect Jørn Utzon were completed in 1973, have since become the pictures people carry in their heads. In reality both look better when you stand under them at dawn, with the ferries just starting up and the water gently moving.

The Grand Pacific Drive begins here, and the sensible way out is south. Leave the centre early on a weekday or Sunday morning, avoid the rush hours, and follow signs through the southern suburbs toward the Royal National Park, which is the second oldest national park in the world, dating from 1879. The road winds through bushland and eucalypt forest with views over the Tasman Sea, and then continues past Stanwell Tops, where hang gliders launch over the cliff. After that comes the Sea Cliff Bridge at Coledale, a curved concrete viaduct built out over the water along a stretch of coast where the old road kept falling into the sea.

Take the traffic seriously. Sydney is a big, busy city, and the tollways around it are electronic, so check how a hire or foreign-registered bike will be billed before you set off. Lane filtering is legal for riders in New South Wales under defined conditions, but local rules are strict and the speed cameras are many, so read up before you rely on it. Summer brings heat, bushfire smoke in bad years and afternoon storms, and the best months for the coast are April to May and September to November.

The city offers everything a rider needs, with fuel at countless stations and workshops for every brand. Spend an evening at the water's edge near Circular Quay, take a ferry across to Manly if you have time, and have a flat white from one of the city's many small roasters. Then the coast road will be waiting.
t.walcha@-31.0,151.6:
Walcha sits on the Northern Tablelands of New South Wales at about a thousand metres, high enough to have real winters, with frosts, a few snowfalls and a cool, clear air that smells of eucalyptus and woodsmoke. The town is small, with about two and a half thousand people, and it wears its sheep country history openly. Fine merino wool built the district, and for a century the big properties around Walcha shaped both the landscape and the social life. English elms and oaks planted in the streets turn gold and red in April, which is not a sight many people expect in Australia.

The town is a showcase of its own idiosyncrasies. Sculptures stand on the main street and elsewhere around the town, the result of a local habit of putting art in public places, and the old buildings along the road recall the days when the wool cheques arrived once a year. Just outside town, Apsley Falls drops into a gorge of dark rock, a short drive and a short walk from the road, and it is a good way to stretch a day.

The Oxley Highway is the reason riders know the name. West of Walcha it crosses the tableland in long open sweeps, with paddocks and granite outcrops, and east of town it begins to tip toward the coast, dropping off the Great Dividing Range in a long series of bends through dense forest and past waterfalls toward Port Macquarie. It is among the better motorcycle roads in the state, and on weekends you will meet other riders. The surface is generally good, though shaded corners stay damp, and logging trucks use the road as well. Watch for kangaroos and wombats at dusk, and for frost in winter mornings.

Walcha has fuel and basic services, but opening hours are those of a country town, so do not count on late-night supplies. The nearest larger centre is Tamworth to the west. Autumn is lovely, with clear days and cool nights, spring brings green paddocks and lambs, and summer can be hot at midday and stormy in the afternoon. Bring a warm layer even then, because the altitude makes the evenings cool.
t.old great north road@-33.4,151.0:
The Old Great North Road is one of the most remarkable pieces of engineering in Australia, and it was built by men who had no choice. Between 1826 and 1836, convicts were set to work cutting a road from the colony at Sydney north to the Hunter Valley, a distance of well over two hundred kilometres, through some of the most broken sandstone country on the continent. They cut deep into the rock with hand tools, built retaining walls of carefully fitted stone, and carried out the work in chain gangs under harsh discipline. The most spectacular surviving section is Devine's Hill, a steep climb with tall dry-stone walls that still look perfect after almost two centuries.

The surviving parts of the road are UNESCO listed as part of the Australian Convict Sites, and the setting is a bushland of sandstone ridges, gum trees, tree ferns in the gullies, and the broad, slow Hawkesbury river in the valley below. At Wisemans Ferry, the road crosses the river by a free cable ferry that runs round the clock, and the crossing itself is a small event, with a short wait and a pleasant clunk of cables. Beyond it, narrow, winding tarmac and gravel climb into Dharug National Park, where you can walk sections of the original road, the walls overgrown with moss and lichen.

For a rider, the roads around here are a mix of twisting sealed sections and unsealed tracks. The surface is not always forgiving, with patched asphalt and loose gravel on the edges, and heavy rain can wash stones across the road. Weekends bring cyclists and cars out from Sydney, so go early in the morning for the quietest riding and the best light. Wildlife, from lyrebirds to wallabies, lives in the bush, and you will hear them as often as you see them.

Fuel is the main practical point. The district has few stations, and Wisemans Ferry has limited supplies, so fill the tank before you come. East Kurrajong, about twenty-three kilometres away, and Kariong on the coast side are the closest larger places. Winter is cool and clear, spring is good, and summer brings heat and the risk of bushfires, when roads can be closed with little warning. Check the fire warnings before you set off in hot weather.
t.greater blue mountains area@-33.7,150.0:
The Blue Mountains are named for a haze. On a warm day, fine droplets of oil released by the eucalyptus forest scatter the blue end of the light and the whole plateau seems to float in a pale mist. The Greater Blue Mountains Area covers about a million hectares of sandstone plateau, deep gorges and sheer cliffs, split into eight protected areas, and UNESCO lists it for the astonishing variety of eucalypts, more than a hundred species, which have adapted to every kind of soil and slope.

This pin lies on the southwestern side, in country around Oberon, which is a very different place from the tourist stretch near Katoomba. The land here is higher, colder and quieter, at over a thousand metres. Frost is common, snow occasionally falls, and pine plantations stand beside native forest. Kanangra Walls, a wall of pale cliffs at the end of a long road, drops into a gorge so deep and broad that the view looks painted. The nearby Jenolan Caves, a spectacular system of limestone chambers, is among the oldest known cave systems in the world and a good wet-weather excuse.

The roads are the attraction for riders. The Jenolan Caves Road descends in a long series of hairpins into the valley, narrow and steep, with tight corners that demand attention. Other roads in the district are quiet, flowing and shaded by tall trees, and the surface ranges from smooth to rough. Kanangra Walls Road is partly unsealed, so check conditions after rain. Fog can fill the valleys at dawn and the temperature drops fast after sunset. Wombats, wallabies and kangaroos graze on the verge at dusk, and a collision with one is a real risk, so make a habit of early starts and early finishes.

Oberon, about thirteen kilometres away, has around three thousand people, with fuel, a bakery and a few places for lunch, and Lithgow, with more than five thousand people, is the larger fallback. Autumn is beautiful, with cool bright days and gold on the introduced trees, while winter can bring ice on shaded bends. Summer can be hot and carries bushfire risk, with closures of roads and parks that can happen quickly.
t.sydney opera house@-33.9,151.2:
The Opera House is the thing that every visitor to Sydney photographs, and it is also a good story about stubbornness and talent. The Danish architect Jørn Utzon won an international competition in 1957 with a design of white sail-like shells rising from the point of land called Bennelong Point. The engineering was so difficult that the building took sixteen years instead of the planned four, costs soared, and a change of government and a dispute with the authorities led Utzon to resign and leave Australia in 1966. He never saw the finished building in person. It opened in 1973, and its tiled shells, covered in thousands of glossy cream and white tiles, have become a symbol of the whole country.

The setting is the point. Sydney Cove, just beside the Opera House, is where the first British fleet landed in 1788 and began a convict colony. The Royal Botanic Garden curves around the next bay, the Harbour Bridge, nicknamed the coathanger, stands over the water, and the old streets of The Rocks, once home to convicts, sailors and dockhands, climb up behind. The Opera House is listed on its own, but it is part of a wider story that includes the convict sites of the colony, such as Hyde Park Barracks, a short walk away.

For a rider the area is for walking, not riding. The roads around Circular Quay are busy with buses, taxis and cyclists, parking is expensive and hard to find, and the motorways have electronic tolls that you should sort out in advance, particularly if you are on a rental. Leave the bike somewhere sensible and take the ferry, which is the best way to see the building, with its roofs changing colour in the light and the whole harbour spread around it.

Fuel stations are plentiful in the suburbs but sparse in the heart of the centre, so fill up on the way in. The best time to visit is early morning, when the forecourt is quiet and the light is gentle, or at dusk, when the sails turn pink and gold. Spring and autumn are comfortable, and summer is hot, humid and crowded, with spectacular thunderstorms over the harbour in the afternoon.
t.mt seaview nature reserve@-31.3,152.2:
Mount Seaview is a high point on the edge of the tableland where the New South Wales Northern Tablelands begin to drop toward the Pacific, and the nature reserve there protects a patch of forest that gets more rain and mist than almost anywhere around. The land is rugged, with steep slopes and tangled gullies, and the vegetation is a blend of dry eucalypt forest on the ridges and cool rainforest in the damp folds. This is the Hastings Range, the eastern flank of the Great Dividing Range, and the forests belong to the larger Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, whose lineage reaches back to the time when the continent was part of a great southern landmass.

The nearby Barrington Tops are a more famous part of the same world. They form a high plateau of wet forest, swamps and old volcanic soil, at over a thousand metres, with Antarctic beech trees that look like something from a fairy tale, covered in moss and draped with ferns. In winter, snow sometimes settles on the tops. Birds are everywhere, from bright king parrots to the thin whip crack of the eastern whipbird in the undergrowth, and leeches are a feature of the wet season, so do not stand still for long in a damp spot.

For riders, the region offers excellent roads. The Oxley Highway slips down off the tableland in a long run of bends, shaded by forest and tinged by mist in the morning, and Thunderbolts Way, named for a bushranger, winds through rolling country and over ridgelines in a quieter, more relaxed way. Surfaces vary, and the combination of damp, shade and gravel on corners calls for attention. Logging trucks use the roads, so take care at blind bends, and watch for wombats and kangaroos at dusk.

There is no settlement at the pin, and the data lists no nearby town, so treat this as a ride through wild country. Fill up at Walcha or Gloucester, depending on your direction, and carry water and a rain jacket. Mobile coverage fades in the gullies. Autumn is the best season, with settled weather and cool, clear mornings, while summer brings hot spells and sudden thunderstorms, and winter brings ice on the shaded tarmac.
t.abu simbel@22.3,31.6:
Abu Simbel is a monument to the vanity of a king and to the stubbornness of engineers. About 1264 BC, the pharaoh Ramesses II ordered two temples to be carved into a sandstone cliff on the west bank of the Nile, far south in Nubia, near what was then the border of Egypt. The larger temple, dedicated to Ramesses himself and to the gods Amun and Ra, has a facade with four seated statues of the king, each about twenty metres high, sitting with a calm and slightly smug expression. The smaller temple, dedicated to the goddess Hathor and to his wife Nefertari, has statues of the queen and king standing at the same scale, a rare honour for a royal wife.

In the 1960s, the building of the Aswan High Dam threatened to drown the temples under the rising waters of what would become Lake Nasser. An international campaign led by UNESCO raised money and mobilised engineers, who cut the temples into huge blocks, moved them uphill and reassembled them inside an artificial mountain, a work that took from 1964 to 1968. The joins are invisible, and the temple even keeps its alignment. Twice a year, around the twenty-second of February and October, the rising sun shines along the whole length of the temple and lights up the statues in the inner sanctuary, except for the god of darkness, who stays in shadow.

Reaching Abu Simbel is part of the adventure. The road from Aswan runs for about two hundred and eighty kilometres across the Nubian Desert, a straight, empty ribbon through sand and rock under a hard blue sky, with a few police checkpoints along the way. Rules about travel in convoys and about foreign vehicles change, so check locally before you set out, and make sure your papers are in order. Heat is severe from May to September, and the best months are November to March. Start before dawn, carry plenty of water and fuel, and watch the sand blowing across the road.

The small town has fuel, a few shops and simple hotels, and the lake gives a view toward the Sudanese border. The ride continues to Wadi es-Sebua, where another temple of Ramesses stands on the lake shore, guarded by an avenue of sphinxes. Wind is a constant, and sandstorms can reduce visibility suddenly. Breathe the dry air, drink tea in the café by the lake, and let the size of the statues sink in.
t.nubian monuments from abu simbel to phil:
Everything at Abu Simbel is a rescue story. Ramesses II had the two rock temples carved into the cliff above the Nile in the thirteenth century BC, with four colossal seated figures of himself guarding the larger one. Then, in the 1960s, the Aswan High Dam was about to drown the whole valley, and an international UNESCO campaign cut both temples into huge blocks and rebuilt them on higher ground, inside an artificial hill. It is one of the great engineering efforts of the twentieth century, and it is the reason a rider can stand here at all, with Lake Nasser glittering off to one side.

The ride that begins here is really a journey north through Nubia's saved monuments, ending at Philae, the temple of Isis, which was likewise lifted off its island and set up on Agilkia. Between them lies the long desert road to Aswan, roughly 280 kilometres of dead-straight tarmac, with the lake sometimes visible and sometimes not. It is not technical riding. The challenge is heat, glare, wind-blown sand on the surface and the sheer emptiness of it. Start before dawn, carry more water than seems sensible, and fill the tank before you leave town, because there is little in between.

Abu Simbel itself is a small place that lives off its temples, with a handful of cafes and guesthouses. Check locally about police convoy rules for the desert road, which have varied over the years. Twice a year, around late February and late October, the morning sun is said to reach all the way into the inner sanctuary of the great temple and light up the seated gods, and the date draws a crowd, so book ahead if that is your plan.

The best hour here is simply early, when the cliff faces are rose-coloured, the tour buses are still on the road and the lake is flat enough to hold the sky.
t.wadi sebua@22.8,32.5:
Wadi es-Sebua means Valley of the Lions, and the name is earned. The temple here, built by Ramesses II, is approached down an avenue of sphinxes, with a colossal statue of the king standing at the front, and then it burrows into the rock behind. The sphinxes have lions' bodies and the faces of the pharaoh, and in the late afternoon their shadows lie long along the sand. Part of the building is freestanding stone, part is cut from the cliff, which makes it feel half temple and half cave.

Like its neighbours in Nubia, it was moved. When the Aswan High Dam filled Lake Nasser in the 1960s, the original site went under, and the temple was taken apart and reassembled on higher ground to the west, a few kilometres away. A smaller Roman-era temple at Dakka and the shrine of Maharraqa were brought to the same place, so you get a little collection of rescued monuments in one stretch of desert above the shore.

There is no town here to speak of, so treat the visit as a pure desert stop. The land is flat, bare and pale, with scattered acacia and the occasional bright green fringe where the lake laps the shore. Wind can be strong, and it carries fine sand that finds its way into zips and visors, so keep your visor shut when you ride in or out. Heat is the main thing; from late spring to early autumn the middle of the day is punishing and the metal of the bike will burn bare skin.

Plan fuel and water from Aswan, which lies far to the north, or from Abu Simbel, and do not count on finding either nearby. Take your time on the approach, because the surface close to the temple is often sandy, and a heavy bike on soft ground is no fun. Then walk the sphinx avenue slowly, once, from the road toward the carved doorway, and you will understand why the builders chose this place.
t.wauchope@-31.5,152.7:
Wauchope sits on the Hastings River in the green country behind Port Macquarie on the New South Wales mid-north coast, a country town of six thousand with a main street of pubs and bakeries, and with a fuel station and a decent meal, so this works as a warm start or a quiet finish. The river flows past the edge of town, and the paddocks are rich dairy and timber land between the coast and the escarpment.

It earns a place on a motorcycle itinerary because the Oxley Highway starts here. Named for the surveyor John Oxley, who explored the area in 1818, the highway climbs west from the coast through rainforest and eucalypt forest onto the New England tablelands towards Walcha, and it has a reputation among Australian riders as one of the better roads in the state. The first stretch above Wauchope is the interesting one: tight and fast bends rising through tall forest, switchbacks in places, and a wet surface under the trees on a cool morning. Take it carefully, because the road has seen serious crashes, and the police are a regular presence, with speed limits that change often and are checked.

Timber shaped the town. In the nineteenth century the cedar-getters and later the loggers worked the hills above the Hastings, and the town grew around the sawmills and the river port; the old timber tradition is part of local memory. Tall brush box and blackbutt still stand in the national parks that line the highway, such as the Werrikimbe wilderness area that the road skirts higher up, and the birdlife is loud at dawn, with lyrebirds and whipbirds in the gullies.

Plan for the weather: summer brings humid heat and sudden thunderstorms, and the tableland above is much colder, so you may start in a T-shirt and finish in a jacket. Fog sits in the valleys in early autumn. Fuel is straightforward in town, but stations thin out after Wauchope on the highway, so top up before you climb. Mornings are best, before the weekend traffic.
t.apsley falls@-31.0,151.8:
Apsley Falls is the place where the gentle New England tableland suddenly falls apart. The Apsley River drifts across open grazing country east of Walcha, and then, without much warning, it plunges over a lip of basalt into a deep gorge that belongs to Oxley Wild Rivers National Park. Standing at the railing, you can feel the spray and hear the water long before you see the base. The gorge walls are layered rock, and the whole scene has the look of a country that was cut open by water over millions of years.

Walcha, seventeen kilometres to the west, is the nearest real town, a tidy tablelands settlement of two and a half thousand people with a reputation for fine merino wool and cool nights. This is high ground, around a thousand metres above sea level, so the air is crisp, frosts arrive early and the mornings often begin in mist. The Oxley Highway, which carries you here, is named after the explorer John Oxley, who crossed this country in 1818 on his search for inland rivers, and it runs east from the tablelands down to the coast at Port Macquarie.

As a ride, the Oxley is one of the better roads in New South Wales, though it has two moods. Up here it is open and rolling, with long sweeping bends over farmland, pale gums, and wide views to the ridge. Further east the road changes character, dropping off the escarpment through forest, with tighter corners and a surface that can be damp and slippery under the trees. Kangaroos and wombats are a real risk at dawn and dusk, so ride during the day if you can. Roadworks and logging trucks add to the picture.

Practical points: Walcha has fuel and cafes, and it is the last sure supply for a good distance, so fill the tank before the long run east. The falls have a short walking track, a picnic area and a campground, which suits a tea break by the river. The best time to be here is autumn, when the air is clear and the grass is gold, or after rain, when the falls are at their strongest and the gorge hums.
t.gingers creek@-31.4,152.2:
Nobody builds a monument to a creek crossing, and Gingers Creek is not one. It is a name on the map along the eastern run of the Oxley Highway, a wet fold of forest somewhere between the cool grazing tablelands around Walcha and the warm coast at Port Macquarie, and the coordinates fall in country with no town of any size nearby. What you get is the landscape itself, which is reason enough to stop.

This is the Great Dividing Range at its eastern edge, where the plateau breaks into steep spurs and gullies that run towards the sea. The vegetation changes by the kilometre. Up on the flatter ground you ride past open eucalypt woodland, tall blackbutt and stringybark with grassy understorey, and as the road drops, it enters pockets of subtropical rainforest, ferns the size of umbrellas, strangler figs, vines hanging like cables. After rain the whole slope drips, and the air smells of wet leaf mould and eucalyptus. The big national parks of this part of New South Wales, such as Werrikimbe and Oxley Wild Rivers, are close by and hold koalas, wallabies, lyrebirds and some of the most remote bushland in the state.

The riding is where the Oxley Highway earns its reputation. This is the section where the road descends the escarpment, with a long sequence of medium and tight bends, some of them blind, climbing and dropping over creeks and spurs. The surface is generally decent but patchy, and in shady corners it can stay damp and covered in leaf litter and bark long after the sun has come out. Logging trucks use the road, and they take their share of the middle, so a hard-braking left-hander behind one of them is something to anticipate rather than find out the hard way. At dawn and dusk, wallabies and kangaroos graze at the verges, and wombats and cattle turn up where you least expect them.

The sure places to fill up are Walcha to the west and the towns near the coast, with little in between, and it pays to leave with a full tank and a bottle of water. Weather matters: mist and fog collect on the escarpment in the cool months, and summer thunderstorms can drop a lot of water fast. Autumn and spring are the most reliable seasons. Pull over where there is room, switch off, and listen: whipbirds crack across the valley and the creek runs invisibly below.
t.nashville@36.2,-86.8:
Nashville is where the Natchez Trace begins in spirit, although the parkway itself starts on the southwestern side of the city, near the town of Pasquo, a short ride from downtown. The city sits on the Cumberland River, in a bowl of rolling Tennessee hills, and has been a centre of music since the Grand Ole Opry began broadcasting from here in the 1920s. Broadway, the strip of honky-tonks in the middle of town, plays live music from morning till late, and the Ryman Auditorium, a former church with pews that still serve as seating, is one of the most respected small concert halls in the country.

The route south is a different animal altogether. The Trace follows an ancient path that began as a game trail and was used by Native Americans, then by Kentucky boatmen who floated goods down the Mississippi to Natchez and walked home. The modern parkway, administered by the National Park Service, runs for 444 miles to Natchez, Mississippi, and has a speed limit of about fifty miles an hour, no commercial traffic, no billboards, and no stoplights. It is a ride for rhythm and calm, with tree canopies, rolling farmland, and a stream of small historical sites, from Native American mounds to Civil War battlefields. Tupelo, the birthplace of Elvis Presley, lies about three hundred miles along.

Deer are a serious hazard at dawn and dusk, and a slow, steady pace is the right approach. In autumn the leaves are brilliant, and in spring the dogwoods bloom along the roadside.

Before you go, spend an evening in the city. Hot chicken, a spicy local fried dish, has become the city's signature meal, and the best places have lines out the door. Centennial Park holds a full-scale replica of the Parthenon, built for the 1897 exposition, and it is a strange and wonderful sight under a Tennessee sky. Fuel, hotels and bike shops are everywhere, and the parkway entrance is a short run down the road.
t.pitkyaranta@61.6,31.5:
Pitkäranta means long shore in Finnish, and the town still carries the name that it had when it belonged to Finland. It lies on the north-western shore of Lake Ladoga, the largest lake in Europe, in the Republic of Karelia, and was a copper and tin mining district from the middle of the nineteenth century. The area was ceded to the Soviet Union after the Second World War, and the Finnish population left. Today it is a town of about thirteen thousand, with Soviet-era apartment blocks, old wooden houses and the weathered remains of the mines in the hills around.

The setting is the main attraction. Ladoga's shoreline here is a maze of granite skerries, islets and narrow bays, covered with pine and spruce, and the water is cold and clear. The rocks are some of the oldest on Earth, rounded and scratched by glaciers, and the light on an evening in June, when it hardly gets dark, is beautiful. Ruskeala, a marble quarry flooded to form a turquoise lake, lies not far west and is one of the best-known sights in the region. Further along the coast is Impilahti, which has a more rural feel.

The roads are quiet and the landscape gentle. They pass through forests of birch and conifer, over granite ridges, and past lakes and bogs, with the surface varying from smooth asphalt to patches of rough pavement. The bends are mild, and traffic is thin outside the towns. Mosquitoes and midges can be fierce from June to August, and winter brings deep snow, so spring and early autumn are best. Moose are common on the roads, particularly at dusk.

Pitkyaranta has fuel, food and shops, and the next larger places, Salmi and Lyaskelya, are around thirty kilometres away. Local specialities include smoked fish from the lake and karelian pasties. Foreign visitors should check carefully what is currently permitted and what documentation is needed before planning a trip here. The pace of life is slow, and the lake sets the rhythm.
t.armidale@-30.5,151.7:
Armidale sits on the New England tableland at close to a thousand metres, which means it feels cooler than anywhere else for hundreds of kilometres around. It is a handsome city of about twenty-four thousand people, with two cathedrals, wide streets lined with deciduous trees that turn gold and red in autumn, and a university that gives it a lively student feel. After the long climb from the coast on the Waterfall Way, it is a welcome place to stop, and it is a proper city, with every service a rider could want.

The Waterfall Way itself is the great attraction. The road runs from Armidale down across the escarpment to Bellingen and Coffs Harbour, passing through some of the most dramatic scenery in New South Wales. At Ebor you can walk to the falls, and the Wollomombi Falls nearby are among the tallest in Australia. The Oxley Wild Rivers National Park cuts deep gorges into the plateau, and further east the Dorrigo National Park holds ancient subtropical rainforest, part of the Gondwana Rainforests World Heritage area. The bends on the descent are tight and rewarding, but the road can be wet, and fog is common on the top.

Armidale's history includes a long record of pastoral wealth, and the old stone buildings in the centre reflect this. The city sits in a district of sheep and cattle country, and the cold winters and frosty mornings are part of local identity. Snow falls on the tableland occasionally, and in winter, black ice is a real concern on the shaded sections of the road.

Fuel is plentiful in Armidale, and there are many cafes and bakeries in the main street, which is closed to through traffic in places. Uralla, a smaller town to the south, is known for its association with Captain Thunderbolt, a bushranger who was shot there in 1870, and is a good stop for a pie.

For the best weather, ride in spring or autumn, when the days are mild and the colours are strong. Summer afternoons bring thunderstorms, and winter mornings can be bitter.
t.coffs harbour@-30.3,153.1:
Coffs Harbour is where the Waterfall Way meets the sea, and the town has the easygoing, banana-and-surf character you expect from the mid-north coast of New South Wales. The Big Banana, opened in 1964 and often credited as Australia's first big roadside novelty, still stands beside the highway as a reminder of the plantations that once covered the hills. These days blueberries have mostly replaced bananas, but the sunny slopes are still there.

Start your day at the harbour, where a breakwater leads out to Muttonbird Island, called Giidany Miirlarl by the Gumbaynggirr people. Wedge-tailed shearwaters, the muttonbirds themselves, nest here from late August to April, and the walk to the top gives a sweeping view up and down the coast and across the Solitary Islands Marine Park. In the cooler months, from about May to November, humpback whales pass offshore and can often be seen from the headland. The harbour jetty is a fine place for an early coffee before the traffic builds.

The riding begins once you leave town. The Waterfall Way climbs from the coastal plain through Bellingen, a leafy riverside village with galleries and bakeries, then rises through the rainforest of the Dorrigo escarpment, where the road twists through tall trees and tree ferns and the air gets noticeably cooler and wetter. Dorrigo National Park has a skywalk over the canopy, and a string of waterfalls, including Dangar Falls, gives the road its name. On the plateau the landscape opens into dairy country and then rolls on to Armidale. The best conditions are in the morning in the dry months, when the road is clear of mist and tourist traffic. Wet roads under rainforest canopy can be slippery with leaf litter, so go gently on the downhill bends.

As a town of more than twenty-six thousand, Coffs Harbour has fuel, food, motorbike shops and accommodation in plenty. The Pacific Highway bypass has pulled most trucks away from the town centre, which makes for easier riding than it used to be.

Fill the tank before you leave: services thin out on the escarpment, and the best stretches are best enjoyed without watching the gauge.
t.dorrigo@-30.3,152.7:
Dorrigo is a quiet town of about a thousand people on a high plateau in northern New South Wales, a dairy and potato district that feels cool and green compared with the coast an hour below. The plateau is the edge of the old volcanic land that rose after the great Gondwana breakup, and it still catches the rain from the Pacific. The result is a rainforest that has survived as an island of tall, dripping trees, now protected in Dorrigo National Park and listed with other east-coast reserves as the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia. A short drive from the town you can walk a boardwalk through the canopy and look down on ferns and strangler figs.

The road to know is the Waterfall Way, which climbs from Coffs Harbour and Bellingen up the escarpment to Dorrigo and continues toward Armidale. The ascent is a long run of bends through forest and farmland, with the road cut into the hillside and the air changing from warm and humid to cool and misty as you climb. The surface is generally good, but the shade keeps it damp, and in wet weather, when fog sits in the trees, the visibility is low. Wildlife is a real hazard: wallabies, wombats and possums come out at dusk, and cattle sometimes wander on the road. Dangar Falls, a pretty drop just outside the town, is an easy stop.

Dorrigo has the feel of a town that is used to riders. Cafes, a bakery, a pub and a fuel station on the main street cater to travellers, and a railway museum and a small steam railway recall the time when trains carried milk and timber down to the coast. Bellingen, twenty-two kilometres down the hill, has a larger choice and an arty atmosphere.

Season matters. Summer brings heavy rain and humidity, with thunderstorms in the afternoon, while winter is dry and clear but can be cold at night on the plateau. Spring has wildflowers and a clean light, which many riders prefer. Leeches live in the rainforest and are harmless but unpleasant, so wear boots on any walk. It is the sort of place where a flat white and a hot pie taste far better than they should.
t.singleton@-32.6,151.2:
Singleton lies in the Hunter Valley on the New England Highway, a coal town in the middle of wine country, with the Hunter River looping through flat green fields on its way to Newcastle. It is not a pretty town in a conventional sense, but it is useful, and for riders finishing the Putty Road, it is the first proper service centre after a long run through the sandstone bush.

The Putty Road itself is one of the best-known motorcycle roads in New South Wales, running about 170 kilometres from Windsor north through Colo and the Wollemi National Park to Singleton. It is a narrow, undulating ribbon through eucalypt forest, with tight bends and long, fast sections, and there are few services along it. That has made it a favourite with Sydney riders, and also with the police, who patrol it heavily and use speed cameras. Treat the limits seriously, because fines and licence points here have ruined a lot of weekends. The road's surface is generally good, but sections can be damp under tree cover, and wildlife, including wallabies, wombats and kangaroos, is common at dawn and dusk.

Singleton's history goes back to the 1820s, when it was founded by Benjamin Singleton on a river flat, and it grew as a service town for the farms and later the coal mines of the upper Hunter. It also hosts a large army base, home to the infantry school, so you see soldiers in town. The big open-cut mines around the district supply much of the export coal that leaves Newcastle, and the haze of dust and the long coal trains are a common sight.

Fuel, food and accommodation are easy in town, which has several petrol stations along the main street and plenty of pubs and bakeries. Pokolbin and the main wine district are less than an hour away, so if you have time the cellar doors, cheese shops and restaurants are an excellent follow-up to a long road.

Fill up in Singleton before heading back down the Putty, because fuel on the road itself is scarce.
t.port macquarie@-31.4,152.9:
Port Macquarie began life as a prison. In 1821 the colonial government established a penal settlement at the mouth of the Hastings River for convicts who had committed further crimes, naming it after Governor Lachlan Macquarie, and the place later became a quiet farming and fishing community before it was reinvented as a holiday town. Today it is a lively coastal city of more than forty thousand, with surf beaches, a long breakwall covered in painted rocks and a pleasant foreshore walk.

The town's best-known resident is the koala, which has its own hospital here, open to visitors and caring for animals injured by cars, dogs and fire. The surrounding bushland still holds a wild population, and you will see road signs warning of them. A few kilometres south, Tacking Point lighthouse looks out over a wide sweep of ocean where humpback whales pass in winter, and the walk to it from the car park is short and easy.

This is where the Oxley Highway Mountain Section begins, and it is a good one. The road leaves the coast and climbs steadily into the Great Dividing Range, with a series of curves through rainforest and eucalypt, passing lookouts and the turn to Ellenborough Falls, one of the longest single-drop waterfalls in the southern hemisphere. Higher up, near Walcha, the landscape opens into tableland farms and cool air. The surface is generally well maintained, though trucks and caravans slow progress on weekends, and fog in the mountains is common in the morning. The highway is named after John Oxley, who explored this country in 1818 and found the Hastings River on his way down to the sea.

For fuel, Port Macquarie has everything, including several big stations on the highway, and the main street has cafés, bakeries and plenty of pubs. Services are sparse once you climb, so fill the tank before leaving. If the weather turns, you can retreat to the Glasshouse arts centre by the river, or watch the dolphins from the breakwall at sunrise.

I would start early, with the sun behind you on the way up, and leave time for a coffee at the top before turning back.
t.cockatoo island convict site@-33.8,151.2:
You cannot ride to Cockatoo Island, and that is part of its charm. The island sits in the Parramatta River at its junction with Sydney Harbour, reached only by ferry, and the pin on the map falls on the nearby shore of Balmain and Birchgrove, where you can park the bike and look across the water at it.

The island was a convict prison from 1841, built to house men who had reoffended in the colony, and the prisoners themselves quarried the sandstone and dug the silos and barracks that still survive. Later it housed a reformatory for girls and then one of the busiest shipyards in the Southern Hemisphere, building and repairing naval ships through both world wars until the yard finally closed in 1991. Its industrial heritage and its convict remains are both visible, and UNESCO included it in the Australian Convict Sites World Heritage listing in 2010.

Balmain, a short ride from the pin, is an old working-class suburb of sandstone cottages and narrow terraced streets that became fashionable in the 1970s and now has a pub on almost every corner. Darling Street, the main road, is lined with cafés, bookshops and old hotels, and the waterfront parks at Birchgrove and Elkington offer a good view across the harbour to the city skyline. The roads are narrow, hilly and often one-way, with parked cars on both sides, and local drivers are impatient, so allow for slow riding and watch for opening doors.

For practicalities, fuel is easy in nearby Rozelle and Leichhardt, and motorbike parking in the inner west is more generous than in the CBD, though it is usually time-limited. The ferry to the island runs from Circular Quay and Barangaroo, and a timetable is easy to find; do check it before making plans, as services vary.

If you can, go late in the afternoon, when the light on the sandstone turns gold, and watch the ferries come and go beneath the Harbour Bridge.
t.hyde park barracks@-33.9,151.2:
Hyde Park Barracks is on Macquarie Street, in the heart of Sydney, in a row of colonial buildings that tell the story of the city's beginning. The barracks were designed by Francis Greenway, himself a convicted forger, and built in 1819 to house about six hundred male convicts who worked on government projects, so the man who drew the plans was the same kind of prisoner who would sleep there. Later it served as an immigration depot for women, an asylum and a courthouse, and it now operates as a museum with hammocks and artefacts that bring the convict years to life.

The setting is worth lingering over. Macquarie Street is lined with grand sandstone buildings, including Parliament House, the old Mint and the State Library, and the adjoining Hyde Park offers a shady retreat between avenues of fig trees, with the Archibald Fountain at one end. St Mary's Cathedral stands to the east, and the Royal Botanic Garden and the Opera House are a short walk away. UNESCO recognised the barracks in 2010 as part of the Australian Convict Sites, and the buildings' geometric Georgian lines are a reminder of how rigidly Sydney's early planners thought.

Riding here needs patience. The CBD has tolls, bus lanes, tram works and some of the most expensive parking in the country, and one-way streets make navigation tricky. Motorcycle parking bays exist in the area, particularly around the Domain, and are often cheaper than cars, but they fill quickly on weekdays. If you are visiting, I would suggest parking in the Domain or at the edge of the city and walking in. Sundays and early mornings are far easier.

Sydney has no shortage of fuel stations, though the city centre itself has few, so fill up in the inner suburbs before you come in. For coffee and lunch, the laneways around Martin Place and the Rocks hold a good supply of cafés and pubs, and the old Queen Victoria Building is nearby.

Walk down to Circular Quay when you are done and watch the ferries cross the harbour. It is the best free show in the city.
Barrington Tops is the high, cold, wet plateau at the top of the Hunter and Manning catchments in New South Wales, and it feels like a different continent from the dry coast an hour to the east. The range is a remnant of an ancient volcanic landscape, and its altitude, well over a thousand metres on the plateau, means snow gums, frost in winter and the odd dusting of snow. It is part of the Gondwana Rainforests World Heritage Area, and the forests here hold Antarctic beech, a tree that was once spread across the ancient southern supercontinent and now survives only in a few cold, damp pockets.

Getting up there is a ride rather than a drive. The main access is from the Scone side, through Moonan Flat and up the Barrington Tops Forest Road, or from Gloucester and Dungog to the east. Much of the plateau road is gravel, narrow and steep, with corrugations and loose stones, and rain can turn parts of it to slick clay. Locals say that if the weather has been bad, you should not attempt it on a heavy bike. Check with the National Parks office or the local visitor centre before going, because sections are closed after storms or fire.

Rewards are high for anyone who makes it. On the tops, snow gum woodland gives way to swampy meadows and mossy rainforest, and the air smells of wet leaves and eucalyptus. Platypus live in the streams, and the forests hold lyrebirds, wombats and pademelons. There are short boardwalks and walking tracks, and campgrounds with basic facilities, including the popular Polblue area. Fenwicks Scrub, a small flora reserve in the same region, protects a patch of subtropical rainforest with giant trees and is a pleasant detour on foot.

Practical planning matters. Mobile coverage is patchy to absent. Temperatures can fall below freezing on clear nights even in autumn, so a warm layer is not an affectation.

If the weather holds, go in autumn, when the beech leaves turn gold and the days are crisp and still, and leave the tarmac behind you.
t.petroglyphs of the white sea@64.5,34.7:
A few kilometres from the town of Belomorsk, where the Vyg river runs out over bare granite on its way to the White Sea, someone about five thousand years ago sat down and started carving. Over time they and their descendants left thousands of figures in the polished rock: reindeer and elk, boats with crews, people on skis, whale hunts, and strange dancing figures that archaeologists still argue about. The main group on the Vyg is called Zalavruga, found in 1926 and recorded in detail over the following decades, and it counts among the finest rock art in northern Europe.

Do not expect a visitor centre with a car park full of coaches. The rocks lie on the river bank near the edge of the forest, and the best time to see the lines is in low sun or just after rain, when the shallow grooves cast shadows. Some panels are covered to protect them, and a local guide or a museum visit in Belomorsk helps a great deal. Allow time to stand and look at the skiers and the boats, because the longer you stare the more sense the scenes make.

The riding here is quiet northern Karelia. The federal road to Murmansk, the R21, carries lorries and cars, but it has long open stretches through pine and bog, with lakes flashing between the trees, and little traffic outside the holidays. The surface can be patchy after winter, so keep an eye out for frost heaves and watch for elk at dusk. Belomorsk, with about twelve thousand people, has fuel and shops, and the Vyg river here also hosts the start of the White Sea Canal, which was dug by prisoners in the early 1930s at terrible cost.

Mosquitoes and black flies are the real hazard from June to August, so carry repellent and keep your visor shut when you stop. The best months are late May to September, and the days in June barely end. Check current travel advice for Russia before making any plans, since conditions for visitors can change.
t.kayali bogaz@40.0,34.6:
The high plateau of northern central Anatolia is a country of rolling hills and red-brown fields, cut by shallow river valleys and scattered with oak scrub. Kayalı Boğaz lies in the rocky ground near the village of Boğazkale, in the district of Çorum, though the scouting label says Cappadocia, which is a good way to the south. I know the label better than the site itself, so rather than make claims I will describe what surrounds it. This is the heartland of the Hittites, the Bronze Age people who ruled a large part of Anatolia from their capital Hattusha, a short distance away, and the area is dotted with outcrops, gorges and fortified hilltops where they built shrines, dams and lookouts.

The riding is quiet and rewarding in an unshowy way. The roads here are narrow farm tracks and secondary tarmac, with long views across steppe, shallow valleys with poplars and a surprising amount of birdlife, including eagles and kites. Surface quality varies, with potholes and loose gravel where tractors have dragged mud onto the road, so keep your speed modest. Little traffic and almost no tourists outside the summer months make it a place to take your time.

Practical things need planning. The nearest bigger towns are Yozgat, Alaca and Sungurlu, each about twenty-five kilometres away, and Boğazkale itself is a small village with a few pensions and restaurants close to the ruins.
