Fill the tank in one of the towns before you head out, carry water and snacks, and be prepared for sun and wind with little shade. In winter this plateau is cold and snowy, and the roads can ice up, while in July and August it is dry and hot.

The light is the best thing about the place. In the early morning and late afternoon, the long shadows pick out every fold in the hills, and the colours of the stone shift from gold to rose. A dinner of lentil soup, grilled meat and fresh bread in a village guesthouse, with the sound of dogs and sheep bells outside, rounds off the day.
t.hattusha the hittite capital@40.0,34.6:
Between about 1600 and 1200 BC, one of the great powers of the ancient world ruled from a town on a rocky slope in the middle of Turkey. Hattusha, the capital of the Hittites, covered a huge area of ridges and ravines, ringed by walls that run for several kilometres over hilltops, with gates guarded by stone lions, a sphinx and a warrior. The Lion Gate and the King's Gate, with its carved figure of a god or king in a short kilt, are the best known, and the Great Temple, a ruined complex of storerooms and shrine rooms, is among the most evocative sites in Anatolia.

The Hittites were not Greeks or Egyptians, which is why they were forgotten until the nineteenth century. Excavations in the early twentieth century uncovered thousands of clay tablets in cuneiform, which included a copy of the treaty signed after the Battle of Kadesh with Egypt, often described as the oldest surviving peace treaty. The empire collapsed around 1180 BC in the great upheavals of the late Bronze Age, and the city was burned and abandoned. UNESCO listed the site in 1986.

The ruins are spread out, so a circular road takes you from one group to the next, about five kilometres in all, with parking areas at the main points. Walking is better than riding between them, because the slopes are steep, but you can ride the loop and leave the bike at each stop. A few kilometres away, the rock sanctuary of Yazılıkaya has carvings of a procession of gods in the open-air chambers, one of the most moving sites in the country. The stone is soft, and the figures, shown in profile in pointed hats, march along the wall toward their meeting.

The countryside here is open, dry and quiet. The nearest towns with fuel and services are Alaca and Sungurlu, each about twenty-five kilometres away, with Yozgat a little further, so fill the tank beforehand. Boğazkale village has a couple of small restaurants and pensions, but nothing grand. Go in spring, when the hills are green and wildflowers cover the slopes, or early autumn, and bring a hat, since there is little shade among the ruins.
t.hattousa and ibikcam forest@40.0,34.6:
The same hillside that holds the Hittite capital also holds a surprising amount of woodland, and that is the story of this stop. The spelling Hattousa is the French form of Hattusha, and the Ibikçam forest, a stand of pine on the slopes around the ruins, is part of the protected landscape that surrounds the site. After days of riding across bare steppe, it comes as a relief to find shade, birdsong and the smell of resin. The forest was planted or preserved in the twentieth century, and it makes the long walks between the monuments far more pleasant.

Take a path through the trees in the early morning, and you may hear woodpeckers and see a fox slipping across the track. The rocky outcrops that the Hittites used for their fortifications are covered in lichen, and wild thyme and sage grow among the stones. In spring the meadows have orchids and poppies, and the air is pleasantly cool even when the plain is hot. It is also a place where visitors can picnic on the grass and rest, which is useful because the nearest town with proper facilities is about twenty-five kilometres off.

Riding here means quiet, easy roads with good views. The tarmac that links the ruins is narrow but usually in decent condition, and traffic is very light. Further out, the valley of the Kızılırmak, the longest river in Turkey, winds through the plateau, and its red banks and wide bends give way to sweeping fields of wheat. Watch for sheep, tractors and the occasional dog that decides to race your bike. Wind picks up in the afternoon on the open ridges.

Fuel is available in Alaca, Sungurlu and Yozgat, all around twenty-five kilometres from the site, and it is wise to fill up before you arrive. A small tea garden near the ruins and a few simple restaurants in the village sell soup, bread and grilled meat. The best seasons are May to June and September to October, and winter, with snow on the pines, is quiet and beautiful but cold.
t.uralla@-30.6,151.5:
Uralla is a small town on the New England Tableland of New South Wales, at about a thousand meters above sea level, and the cold is something you can feel in the clear air. The high plateau is a landscape of rolling grassland, granite outcrops and sheep paddocks, with winter frosts that can be savage and summers that are mild. The town lies on the New England Highway, just south of the university city of Armidale, and its main street retains the verandas and brick shopfronts of a nineteenth-century gold-and-wool settlement.

Uralla's claim to fame is a bushranger. Frederick Ward, who called himself Captain Thunderbolt, robbed coaches and travelers across the tableland for six years in the 1860s, known for his courtesy and his skill with horses, and he became something of a folk hero. In May 1870 he was shot dead by a policeman near Uralla, and his body was displayed in town. His grave is in the local cemetery, and a life-size statue of him on his horse stands in the main street. A museum in an old mill, McCrossin's Mill, tells the story of the town.

The road that carries his name, Thunderbolts Way, runs from Uralla southeast through Walcha and Nowendoc to Gloucester, about three hundred kilometers of twisting back road that crosses the high country and then drops through rainforest toward the coast. For riders, it is a delightful, quiet route, with long, flowing bends, steep descents and few other vehicles. The surface varies, with some rough patches and a few unsealed sections near the old gold fields, and the weather can change quickly on the plateau.

Uralla has fuel, a supermarket, bakeries and pubs, and Armidale, 22 kilometers north, has more. Walcha, the next town on the Way, is smaller, so fill the tank before leaving. The best months are spring and autumn, with mild days, while summer afternoons can bring thunderstorms and bushfire smoke. Winter mornings bring ice on the road, especially in shaded dips. Kangaroos, wombats and cattle are a serious hazard at dawn and dusk, and the Way has long stretches without mobile coverage.
t.wisemans ferry@-33.4,151.0:
Wisemans Ferry sits where the Hawkesbury River turns through a deep sandstone gorge about an hour north-west of Sydney, and the crossing has been working since the 1820s. Solomon Wiseman, a convict who became a successful businessman, ran the ferry and gave the place its name. Today, a pair of free vehicle ferries, cable-guided and run by the state, carry cars and bikes back and forth across the river around the clock, with a short queue at busy times. It is a pleasing piece of old-fashioned travel, and on a bike there is something neat about rolling onto the steel deck with the river water slapping underneath.

The land around is rugged. Dense eucalypt bush, steep cliffs and the green river fill the view, with Dharug National Park on one side and Yengo National Park beyond. The Hawkesbury is broad and quiet here, a drowned river valley, and the cliffs reflect in the water on still mornings. Kookaburras laugh from the trees, lyrebirds scratch in the undergrowth, and in spring the bush is full of wildflowers and wattle.

The ride takes in the Old Great North Road, a remarkable piece of engineering built by convicts in the 1820s and 1830s to link Sydney with the Hunter Valley. Sections of the stone-walled road survive in the bush, with retaining walls, drains and culverts that are still intact. Some are sealed, some are gravel, and some are for walkers only, so do not assume that every bit is open to bikes. The roads on either side of the river, such as Settlers Road and the road to St Albans, wind in long curves through the valley, with good surfaces and little traffic outside weekends. On weekends, riders come from all over Sydney, so this is a busy place on a sunny Sunday.

Services here are limited. The village has a pub, a store and a caravan park, but fuel is something to organise in advance, because the main towns are some distance away. Windsor and Berowra Heights are the sensible places to fill up. Summer can be hot and bushfire-prone, with road closures in dry spells. The cooler months are the best time, with clear air and soft light on the sandstone.
t.wollombi food@-32.9,151.1:
Wollombi lies in the folds of the hills between the Hunter Valley and the Hawkesbury, a small village that seems to have been overlooked by the twenty-first century. It sits where the Wollombi Brook meets Congewai Creek, with sandstone buildings, a historic pub and a church, all at the crossroads of the old convict road. The Wollombi Tavern, dating from the nineteenth century, is the centre of village life, and a good place to eat and drink, with a verandah where riders and locals sit side by side.

The Great North Road runs through the area, and the history of the village is bound up with it. Convicts built the road in the 1820s and 1830s to link Sydney to the Hunter, working in chains with hand tools, and the quality of the surviving stonework still impresses. Wollombi was once a thriving staging post, with coaches changing horses and travellers staying overnight. The Aboriginal name is thought to mean meeting of the waters, and the Wonnarua people lived in the district for thousands of years before settlement.

The road to the village is a rider's treat. The Wollombi Road winds through bush, dry creek beds and farmland, with steady curves, a few crests and quiet traffic during the week. At weekends, the roads fill with motorcyclists, cyclists and wine tourists on their way to Pokolbin, and you should be wary of cars cutting corners. The surface is mostly good, though the verges are soft and there is gravel where side roads join. Wildlife is a hazard, particularly at dawn and dusk, when kangaroos and wallabies come out to feed.

The countryside is a mix of eucalyptus forest, grazing and vineyards, and in spring there are wildflowers. In summer, it is hot and dry, with a risk of bushfires, and in winter, nights can be cold. The best seasons are autumn and spring.

Food in the village includes the tavern, plus a few cafes and bakeries that cater to travellers. Opening times can be limited on weekdays, so it is worth planning your lunch. Cessnock, about twenty-three kilometres away, is the nearest large town, and has stations, supermarkets and the services you need. From there, the vineyards of the Hunter are only a short run away.
t.hunter valley roads@-32.8,151.3:
The Hunter Valley is the oldest wine region in Australia, with vines planted in the early nineteenth century, and the country around Pokolbin is where most of the cellar doors, restaurants and weekend cottages cluster. It lies about two hours north of Sydney, in a broad valley of gentle hills below the long blue line of the Brokenback Range, and the landscape of vineyards, paddocks and eucalypts is as much of an escape for city people as it was for their grandparents. Semillon, which here matures into a lemony, toasty white with age, is the local speciality, and Shiraz does well too.

The valley is also coal country. Open-cut mines and power stations lie a short distance up the road, and the town of Cessnock grew as a mining centre, so wine, heavy industry and horse studs sit side by side. Wollombi, a village in the hills to the south, has an old inn, a sandstone church and a stretch of the Great North Road, a convict-built route from the 1830s, with retaining walls and culverts in stone that have survived nearly two centuries.

For riders, the backroads around the valley are the draw. Lanes wind between vineyards, with gentle rises and bends, and the main roads through the hills toward Wollombi and Broke carry less traffic. The sealed surface is mostly good, though some minor roads have gravel patches and potholes after heavy rain. Kangaroos and wallabies are common at dawn and dusk, and a collision with one can be serious, so slow down in the evening. Weekends, especially long weekends, bring crowds of visitors and a lot of slow traffic, so a weekday ride is more relaxing.

Cessnock, eight kilometres away, is the main town, with fuel stations, supermarkets and cafes, and it is the safest place to fill up. Several of the wineries serve lunch, though riders will be limiting themselves to a taste at most. Summers can be very hot, with temperatures above forty degrees, and bushfire smoke occasionally affects the region. Autumn and spring are the best seasons, with pleasant temperatures and the vines changing colour in April and May.
t.bells line of road@-33.5,150.5:
Bells Line of Road crosses the Blue Mountains from Richmond to Lithgow, and it is the quieter, more charming alternative to the Great Western Highway. It is named after Archibald Bell, who found the route over the mountains in 1823, a tougher and less direct way than the one used by Blaxland, Lawson and Wentworth ten years earlier. Today it is a good two-lane road, running along a high ridge between sandstone gorges, with eucalyptus forest and fruit orchards, and the traffic is a fraction of that on the highway.

The road begins on the Cumberland Plain and climbs steeply at Kurrajong Heights, with views back across the flat land toward Sydney on a clear day. It then follows a ridge, and its corners are broad and easy, with a few tighter ones on the climbs. The surface is usually good, and the speed limits are strictly enforced, with police patrols common on weekends. Bilpin, in the apple country, is the place for roadside stalls selling apples, cider, pies and fresh juice, especially in autumn. Mount Tomah Botanic Garden, a high-altitude annex of the Royal Botanic Garden, grows cool-climate plants, with rhododendrons, rare conifers and a beautiful display in spring.

The scenery is the Blue Mountains at its grandest. To the south lies the Grose Valley, a vast gorge, and to the north the wild country of Wollemi National Park. This is where the Wollemi pine, a tree thought to be extinct until it was found in a hidden canyon in 1994, still grows. The blue haze that gives the mountains their name comes from oil droplets released by eucalyptus trees, which scatter blue light in the air.

Weather here changes quickly. Winters are cold, with frost and occasionally snow at the highest points, and fog can shroud the road in the mornings. In summer, bushfires can close the road, and the fires of 2019 and 2020 burned much of the surrounding bush. Check traffic and fire alerts before setting off.

Fuel is available at Richmond and Lithgow, and in some of the villages along the way, but opening hours vary, so fill up at either end. Cafes are scattered along the road, and tend to be crowded on weekends. A weekday morning, in autumn or spring, is the best time to take the road.
t.mount victoria@-33.6,150.3:
Mount Victoria is the last village before the Blue Mountains drop away to the west, a handsome, slightly worn place on the crest of the ridge, with a main street of antique shops, cafes and old guesthouses. The village is heritage-listed, and gives the sense that the railway era has never entirely ended. The railway station, with its wide verandahs, is still the centre of the village, and the old station buildings hold a small museum. The Victoria and Albert Guesthouse, a Victorian building, has been welcoming travellers for well over a century.

The history here is the history of getting across the mountains. In the early 1830s, Major Thomas Mitchell built Victoria Pass, a steep descent into the Hartley Valley, using convict labour. The road still follows his line, with the stone retaining walls worn by almost two centuries of traffic, though the modern highway uses a wider alignment. Below lies the Hartley Historic Site, a tiny village of sandstone buildings in a grassy valley, with a courthouse and old inns, now preserved by the state.

For a rider, the village is a rest stop, a place to stop for coffee and cake after the grind of the highway. The stretch from Blackheath up to Mount Victoria is a mix of fast curves and some traffic, the Great Western Highway being a busy road with heavy trucks. The descent of Victoria Pass is steep, with tight bends and trucks on the way down, so approach it carefully, and in wet weather watch the surface. Quieter roads lead off toward the Megalong Valley and the Jenolan Caves, and they are among the best in the district.

At nearly a thousand metres above sea level, Mount Victoria can be cold even when Sydney sweats. Mornings in winter are frosty, and in summer afternoon storms roll in over the ridge. Clouds can fill the valleys below, and it is quite a sight when they do.

Cafes and bakeries are plentiful, and a pie and a coffee on a cold day is hard to beat. Fuel is limited in the village, with Blackheath, six kilometres away, and Lithgow, fifteen, the safer options.
t.three sisters lookout@-33.7,150.3:
The Three Sisters are three tall sandstone pillars standing at the edge of the Jamison Valley, and the lookout at Echo Point is where almost everyone goes to see them. They are the best-known sight of the Blue Mountains, and Katoomba, only a short distance away, has grown up around the view. The rock formations are the remnants of a plateau worn away by wind and water over millions of years, and they are floodlit at night. The cliffs fall away hundreds of metres into the valley, with eucalyptus forest filling the space below.

The Gundungurra people tell a story of three sisters who were turned to stone to protect them from a rival tribe, and the story is told in various forms. In the nineteenth century, the town grew as a coal mining and railway centre and later as a mountain resort, drawing visitors from Sydney by rail. The grand hotels and art deco cafes in Katoomba's main street are legacies of this era. Scenic World, with its steep railway, cableway and skyway, gives other views of the cliffs.

The blue haze is a real thing. Eucalypt trees release fine droplets of oil into the air, and these scatter the blue part of sunlight, giving the valleys their tint. On a clear morning, it is easy to see, and the light on the cliffs is warmest soon after sunrise. Fog and cloud also fill the valley, and the Three Sisters sometimes vanish entirely, which can disappoint visitors but make a good story.

For a rider, Echo Point is a destination rather than a ride. The streets around the lookout fill with coaches and cars, and parking is limited and metered, so arriving early, before the tour buses, is wise. The road from Katoomba to Echo Point is short and slow. A little further on, Cliff Drive and the roads through Leura, with their garden shops and cafes, are more relaxed.

Fuel is easy in Katoomba, which is large enough to have several stations, and there are cafes and restaurants all along the main street. Take a jacket, because even in summer, the wind at the lookout can be cold. Winter often brings clear, sharp light after rain, and it is the least crowded season.
t.bells@-33.5,150.5:
Bells Line of Road is the quieter way over the Blue Mountains, and the one riders in Sydney tend to prefer. It leaves the Hawkesbury lowlands at Richmond and climbs onto the sandstone plateau by way of Kurrajong Heights, then rides the spine of the range across to Lithgow, with none of the shopping strips and traffic lights of the Great Western Highway. It is named after Archibald Bell, a young colonial settler who found a way across the mountains by following Aboriginal tracks in 1823, in a time when the ranges were considered a barrier to the colony's growth.

The character of the road changes as you climb. Orchards of apples and stone fruit come first around Bilpin, with roadside stalls selling cider, pies and bags of apples in autumn. Then the road threads through tall eucalypt forest and heathland, past rocky outcrops and sudden gaps with views down into the valleys of the Grose and Colo, the walls of pale sandstone cliffs dropping away into blue haze. Near Mount Tomah, at about a thousand metres, the air is cooler, and the botanic garden there grows cool-climate plants from around the world, with rhododendrons and a long view out over the ridges.

For riding, the Bells Line is a delight and a slight test. The bends are long and flowing, the surface is generally good, and traffic is lighter than on the highway, but weekends bring many bikes and cars, so overtaking requires care. Fog and cold are real at the top, and in winter there can be ice or even snow, so carry a warm layer. Kangaroos, wallabies and wombats appear at dusk, and fires in dry summers can close the road.

Fuel is the thing to plan. There are stations at Kurrajong and around Richmond on the Sydney side and at Lithgow on the far side, with limited options in between, so fill up before you climb. Pie shops and cafes at Bilpin are a reliable stop. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; summer can bring heat, smoke and big crowds, while winter mornings may be bitingly cold.
t.memphis@35.1,-90.0:
Memphis is the one city on the Great River Road that really demands more than a coffee stop. It sits on a bluff above the Mississippi, where the river bends wide and brown, and it has a bigger claim on American music and history than almost any place its size. Before you ride in, decide how much time you have, because an afternoon is not enough, and a day is only a decent beginning.

The music is the main thing. Beale Street has been a centre of blues for more than a century, and the nearby Sun Studio is where Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Jerry Lee Lewis, and others made early recordings. Graceland, Presley's house, is a short ride south, and Stax Records, the soul label, has a museum that tells a different, equally important story. Memphis is also where Martin Luther King was killed in 1968, and the National Civil Rights Museum, in the former Lorraine Motel, is a serious, moving place that stays with you.

For riders, the great river is the other attraction. The Great River Road follows the Mississippi through ten states, and around Memphis the city's bridges carry you over the water in a way that makes its scale plain. Traffic is that of any big American city, so expect busy highways, heavy trucks, and the occasional pothole. Riding in is not a pleasure but a means of arrival. Outside the city, on either side of the river, the roads turn quieter, with flat farmland, levees, and cypress swamps.

Practicalities are easy: fuel, food, hotels, and bike shops are everywhere, so this is the place for any repair or restock. Food needs a mention. Memphis is known for its slow-smoked ribs and pulled pork, served with a dry rub or a sweet, tangy sauce, and the barbecue joints, from the grand to the grubby, are part of the experience. Summers are very hot and sticky, with thunderstorms and the occasional tornado warning. Spring and autumn are the best times to visit, with milder weather and a pleasant light over the river.
t.impilahti@61.7,31.2:
Impilahti was a Finnish parish until the Second World War, and the name still hangs over this corner of northern Ladoga like an old coat on a hook. Today the area belongs to the Republic of Karelia, and the nearest towns are Lyaskelya and Pitkyaranta, both small industrial settlements strung along the lake. The coordinates sit among forest, rock and water: Ladoga, the largest lake in Europe, is only a short distance off, and its northern shore dissolves into skerries, hundreds of low granite islands and narrow channels that look more like the Baltic coast of Finland than anything inland.

The geology is the story. This is the edge of the Baltic Shield, some of the oldest rock in Europe, scraped bare by ice and left as rounded pink and grey granite, with pines clinging to every crack. Between the outcrops are bogs, small lakes and birch forest, and in the evening the light on the water is long and soft. The Ladoga skerries are also a seal habitat: the Ladoga ringed seal is a freshwater species found nowhere else, and it is rare enough that you should not expect to see one from the road.

The history is layered and sad in the usual border way. Before 1940, this was Finnish Karelia, with Lutheran and Orthodox communities, and farms and fishing villages. After the Winter War and the Continuation War, the population left and the land passed to the Soviet Union, and new settlers came in from other regions. Pitkyaranta, a few kilometres up the shore, grew around mines that produced copper and tin in the nineteenth century, and the old workings and spoil heaps are still part of the landscape. Memorials and old cemeteries are scattered about, and many have been neglected.

The ride follows narrow roads through forest and past small lakes, with long straights between low rises and the odd tight bend around a rock. Surfaces vary, and I would not assume anything about the quality of side roads, especially after the spring thaw. Mosquitoes and blackflies are fierce from June to August. The best months are late May, early June, and September, when the air is clear and the leaves turn.

For fuel, aim for Pitkyaranta, the nearest sizeable town, about nineteen kilometres off, and fill up before heading to the water. Shops and cafés are simple but friendly. Stop where the road meets the shore, and look at the islands. They are the quiet heart of the place.
t.segezha@63.7,34.3:
Segezha is a paper town, and you smell it a few minutes before you see it. It sits on the Vyg River at the southern end of Lake Vygozero, in forest and lake country that has supplied Russia with timber for centuries, and the huge pulp and paper mill by the water has been the town's reason for being since the 1930s. About thirty thousand people live here, in a mix of Soviet apartment blocks, wooden houses and some leafy streets that run down toward the river. It is not a pretty place, but it is a real one, with the manners of a working town, and a good supply stop on the long highway to the White Sea.

The history is partly written in that mill. Before the Revolution there was only a small settlement here, but the timber and the river made it attractive to industry, and the great plant grew steadily with new equipment through the Soviet years. Today it is a part of one of Russia's largest forestry groups, and the logging trucks that rattle down the highway are part of the same chain. The forest around is spruce, pine and birch, dotted with lakes and bogs, and the autumn colour in September is fine.

For a rider, Segezha is on the main road north, the highway that links St Petersburg to Murmansk, and the surface here is generally good, with long straights, forest on both sides, and a steady procession of lorries. Care is needed in wet weather, because the dark asphalt gets slick, and deer and elk sometimes wander across at dusk. Summer brings long light and biting insects, and winter is long and snowy. The best months are June to September.

Fuel and food are easy. The town has several stations, supermarkets, cafés and a few hotels, so it makes a natural place to fill up and eat before pressing on. Nadvoitsy, about fourteen kilometres north, has its own aluminium smelter and the falls of the Vyg, which are worth a look if you have time. The Belomorsk-Baltic Canal runs through the area, linking Lake Onega with the White Sea, and traces of it appear along the road.

Eat a proper meal, buy some water, and watch the light on the river. It is quiet and honest.
t.belomorsk@64.5,34.8:
Belomorsk is the town at the northern end of one of the most notorious building projects in Soviet history. The White Sea-Baltic Canal, which runs more than two hundred kilometres from Lake Onega to the White Sea, was dug in the early 1930s in just twenty months, largely by hand, by prisoners of the Gulag. Tens of thousands of them died in the process, from cold, hunger and exhaustion, and the canal, though celebrated by propaganda at the time, turned out to be too shallow for most large ships. The last lock stands at Belomorsk, where the Vyg River meets the sea, and it is hard to look at it without thinking of the cost.

The town was called Soroka before 1938, a Pomor fishing and trading settlement on the western shore of the White Sea, and the old name still appears in local speech. About twelve thousand people live here, in a mix of wooden houses, Soviet blocks and the industrial buildings of the port. It has a small, grey, seaside feeling, with cranes, rail sidings, a sawmill smell and a cold wind off the water. The sea itself is shallow and tidal only a little, and in winter it freezes solid.

Far older than anything modern are the petroglyphs near the town, carved into the granite shore by Stone Age hunters about five thousand years ago. The Belomorsk rock carvings show elk, boats, hunters, and dancing figures, and they are part of the same tradition as those at Lake Onega. They are on the UNESCO tentative list in a group, and there is a small museum in town that tells the story, though I would check the opening times before you go.

The road here, part of the main highway to Murmansk, is a good modern surface with long straights, forest and the odd stretch of roadworks. Heavy lorries are the main hazard, and rain makes the road slick. Summer days are long, and mosquitoes are fierce in July. September is quiet and golden, and the sea air is clean and cold.

Fuel is no problem, with several stations in town, as well as shops, cafés and a couple of hotels. It is a good place to fill up before heading north toward the coast. Walk down to the lock if you can, and spend a quiet minute there.
t.belize barrier reef reserve system@17.2,:
There is no road here, and there never will be. The coordinates put you in open Caribbean water off the coast of Belize, among the atolls and cayes that make up the Belize Barrier Reef Reserve System, a chain of seven protected areas inscribed together as a World Heritage site. The reef runs for about three hundred kilometres along the coast and is the largest barrier reef in the northern hemisphere. Charles Darwin, who never saw it himself, described it from reports as the most remarkable reef in the West Indies. Beyond the main barrier lie three atolls, rare in the Caribbean, including Lighthouse Reef with its famous Great Blue Hole, a perfectly round underwater sinkhole that Jacques Cousteau made famous in the early 1970s.

So for a rider, this is the point where the bike stays on land. Belize City is the main jumping-off point, along with the town of Dangriga further south and the islands of Caye Caulker and Ambergris Caye, which are reached by water taxi. Leave the bike somewhere secure on the mainland and take a boat. Divers and snorkellers can see turtles, nurse sharks, rays, enormous schools of fish and coral gardens; on Half Moon Caye, a colony of red-footed boobies nests in the trees. West Indian manatees graze in the shallow lagoons closer to the shore.

The riding in Belize itself is short but varied. The country is small and the main roads, such as the George Price Highway west towards the Guatemalan border and the Hummingbird Highway south-east to Dangriga, are the highlights. The Hummingbird, in particular, winds through the Maya Mountains with jungle on both sides, citrus plantations and limestone hills, and is considered one of the most scenic roads in Central America. Expect speed bumps in villages, sudden potholes and slow-moving trucks. English is the official language, which makes things easy.

Fuel and supplies are available in Belize City, Dangriga and Belmopan, the capital. The hurricane season runs from June to November and the rainy season can make some secondary roads muddy and slow, so the best time to visit is between late November and April. Try rice and beans with stewed chicken, fresh conch in season and a cold local beer after a day on the water.
t.new england national park@-30.5,152.5:
At Point Lookout, on the edge of the New England tableland in northern New South Wales, the land drops away so suddenly that on a clear morning you seem to be standing on the rim of the world. The escarpment falls more than a kilometre to the Bellinger valley, and on many days a sea of cloud fills the valleys below, with the ridges sticking out like islands. New England National Park protects this edge of the Great Dividing Range, and it is part of the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia, a World Heritage site that preserves forests whose lineage goes back to the time when Australia was part of the supercontinent of Gondwana. Here grow Antarctic beech trees, gnarled and draped with moss, in a cool temperate rainforest that feels more like a fairy tale than Australia.

The park ranges from snow gum woodland and heath at the top, often over fifteen hundred metres, to subtropical rainforest at the bottom of the escarpment. Lyrebirds scratch in the leaf litter, and the call of the bellbird rings through the forest. The weather on top is unpredictable: fog, rain and cold winds are common, and in winter snow is possible.

For riders, the park lies on one of the great roads of Australia: the Waterfall Way, which runs from Armidale on the tableland through Wollomombi and Ebor to Dorrigo and down to Bellingen and the coast near Coffs Harbour. Along the way, waterfalls such as Wollomombi, Ebor and Dangar Falls plunge into gorges, and the descent from Dorrigo to Bellingen is a long series of bends through the rainforest. The road into the park itself is partly unsealed and can be rough or muddy after rain. Wildlife, especially wallabies and kangaroos, is common on the roads at dawn and dusk, and the tableland can be foggy.

There are no services in the park, and very few along the road, so fill up in Armidale or Dorrigo, which are a long way apart. Ebor has a small store and a pub. There are campgrounds and cabins in the park for those who want to stay. Dorrigo has cafés and bakeries, and Bellingen, at the foot of the escarpment, is a relaxed town with a good market. Bring warm clothes even in summer, because it can be cold on the tableland.
t.historic centre of saint petersburg and:
Saint Petersburg began here, on Hare Island in the Neva, where Peter the Great laid the foundations of the Peter and Paul Fortress in 1703. The fortress, with its tall golden spire above the cathedral where Russian emperors are buried, still marks the heart of the city, and from its walls you look across the river to the Winter Palace, the Hermitage and the long granite embankments that make the city one of the most beautiful in Europe. The historic centre and its related monuments form a World Heritage Site.

The city is built on islands and canals, with palaces, churches and grand avenues laid out by Italian, French and Russian architects in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Nevsky Prospekt, the main avenue, runs from the Admiralty to the Alexander Nevsky Monastery. In June, the white nights mean that it never gets fully dark, and the city stays awake late into the night.

For riders, the city has one crucial rule: the bridges. During the navigation season, from spring to autumn, the bridges over the Neva are raised at night to let ships pass, and if you are on the wrong side when they open you will be stuck until they close again in the early morning. Check the schedule and plan accordingly. Traffic in the centre is heavy, cobbles and tram lines are common, and parking can be difficult.

Across the Kronverk strait from the fortress lies the Petrograd side, where the city's grand apartment blocks, many in Art Nouveau style, line the avenues, and the cruiser Aurora, whose gun gave the signal for the storming of the Winter Palace in 1917, is moored on the Bolshaya Nevka. A walk around the fortress walls, with the noon cannon fired from the Naryshkin bastion every day, is the classic introduction. On sunny days people sunbathe against the warm granite of the walls by the river, even in early spring with ice still floating past.

Fuel and services are everywhere. A foreign rider has extra homework at present, from visas to the fact that most Western cards fail at the pump. The best time to visit is in summer, when the weather is mild and the days are long, but crowds are heavy. Spring and autumn are quieter, though weather can be grey and wet.
t.the e i lopukhina s@60.1,30.3:
North of Saint Petersburg's centre, the city thins out into a mix of suburbs, dachas, pine woods and the long marshy shores of the Karelian Isthmus. The label here refers to an estate of the Lopukhin family, and I do not know enough about it to describe what stands on the spot, so I will tell you about the country around it, which is Levashovo, Pargolovo and Sertolovo, a few kilometres in each direction.

This was dacha country from the nineteenth century, when wealthy Petersburgers built summer houses among the pines and the lakes, many in carved timber with verandas and little towers. Pargolovo kept some of these, with its old parks and ponds, though many have been replaced by newer homes. At Levashovo, a wooded area to the south, a memorial cemetery marks the Levashovo Wasteland, where thousands of people executed in the Stalin purges of the 1930s were buried in secret. It is a quiet, solemn place with rows of graves, and it is worth stopping if you are in the area.

In the autumn of 1941 the city was surrounded and the front line ran along this part of the isthmus. The Finnish army stood to the north, the Red Army dug in around the city, and a ring of defensive works, trenches, batteries and forts, was built in the woods, a part of what the Russians call the Blockade Ring. Some remains survive, mostly as earthworks and concrete shelters overgrown with moss, and a few have been made into memorials. The southern batteries listed on your ride belong to that same story.

As for riding, the roads are straight and fairly busy with city traffic, and surfaces vary from smooth new asphalt to patched older sections. The Priozerskoe and Vyborg highways, the main routes north, are heavy with trucks and commuters, and the pleasant riding is on the smaller roads through the pine woods, where birch leaves turn yellow in September and the air smells of resin and wet moss. Winter is long and dark, and snow lies from November until April.

Pargolovo, with twelve thousand people, and Sertolovo, with forty-three thousand, have petrol stations, shops and cafes, and the whole area is part of the metropolitan region, so nothing is far away. Check current travel rules for foreign visitors before you plan anything here.
t.vyborgskaya road@60.1,30.3:
Every road out of Saint Petersburg to the north-west ends up in Finland or in the memory of it, and the Vyborg highway is the old way. It leaves the city through the northern suburbs of Shuvalovo, Pargolovo and Parnas, passing parks, lakes and rows of tower blocks, and then continues over the Karelian Isthmus to Vyborg, a town that belonged to Finland until 1940.

The isthmus has been a war zone more often than it deserves. Before the Winter War of 1939 and 1940, the Finnish border ran along the little river Sestra, only some thirty kilometres from the centre of Leningrad, and the city's northern outskirts were within reach of artillery. During the siege of the city from 1941, the front stood just beyond this area, and the Blockade Ring of trenches, concrete batteries and earth forts was dug through the woods. The names on your ride, such as Northern Battery No. 4 and Petrovsky, belong to this chain of defences. In the summer, you can still find overgrown earthworks and the rusty remains of gun positions in the forest beside the paths, though I cannot say which are accessible from the point you have marked.

Shuvalovo is named after a noble family who owned land here, and the area around the Lakes of Ozerki has long been popular for summer walks. Parnas, a neighbourhood of tall apartment blocks, is not a place for sightseeing. The best use of this stop is to see the nearer side of the city's northern defences and then to ride on into the quieter forest country a little further north.

The riding itself is plain. The main highway is wide, fast and full of lorries and commuters, with speed cameras and sudden changes in speed limits, and the pleasant riding is on the side roads through the pine woods, where silver birch and sand dunes give the isthmus a Finnish feeling. Winter is long and the roads are icy from November to March, while late June, with its white nights, is the most memorable season. Mosquitoes and ticks are numerous in the woods in summer, so wear long sleeves.

Shuvalovo has about six thousand people, with a handful of shops and petrol stations, and Parnas and Pargolovo have more, so fuel and a quick meal are easy. Local food leans toward soup, dumplings and sour cream, and the cafes along the highway are cheap and plain. Check the rules for foreign travellers in Russia before you plan a trip.
t.mt hyland nature reserve@-30.2,152.4:
Ask a New South Wales local about Mt Hyland and you may get a shrug, which is partly the point. The nature reserve occupies high, cool country on the edge of the New England tableland, west of the Dorrigo plateau, in the same belt of mountains that holds the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia. Here the forest changes character as you climb: warm eucalypt forest gives way to tangled rainforest and then to stands of Antarctic beech, gnarled and moss-draped trees whose relatives grow in Patagonia and New Zealand, a leftover from the days when the southern continents were joined.

The nearest town is Dorrigo, a little over thirty kilometres away, and there is nothing resembling a service station in the reserve itself. Fill the tank in Dorrigo or on the New England side in Armidale, which is a much bigger town. Around here the distances between pumps are real, and mobile coverage drops out quickly. Carry water, a spare layer and a decent map.

Riding in this district means choosing your surface with care. The sealed Waterfall Way, which climbs from the coast through Dorrigo and Ebor, is a superb road, with sweeping gradients, bends in tall forest, waterfalls at Ebor, and the sort of morning mist that lets you feel the altitude. The tracks that climb toward the reserve itself are another matter: gravel, ruts and washouts, passable by a trail bike in dry weather and a bad idea after heavy rain. Only go if you have the right machine and the skills.

The air at this height is cold, even in summer, and winter nights drop below freezing, with the occasional light snowfall. The rain forest is wet most of the year, rich with ferns, lichens and the calls of bowerbirds and whipbirds. Spring and autumn offer the best compromise of mild days and dry tracks. Leave no litter, stay on formed tracks, and treat the beech stands carefully: some of the oldest trees are several centuries old, and they grow slowly.
t.old government house and domain@-33.8,15:
Few buildings in Australia can claim to be as old as this one. Old Government House sits in Parramatta Park, on a rise above the Parramatta River, and was begun in 1799 under Governor Hunter. It is the oldest surviving public building in the country, a plain, graceful Georgian house where successive governors lived and worked, including Lachlan Macquarie, who added to the estate. It forms part of the UNESCO listing of Australian Convict Sites, which recognises how the penal colony shaped the nation.

The reason for the site lies in the river. Parramatta, from the Burramattagal word often said to mean the place where eels lie down, was the second European settlement in Australia, founded in 1788 because the soil beside the river was better than at Sydney Cove. The Burramattagal people had lived here for thousands of years, fishing and gathering along the same water. The park, which was once the governor's domain, still carries that double history in its old trees and open lawns.

For riders it is an easy and civilised stop in the middle of a big city. Parramatta is Sydney's second heart, and Westmead is right beside the park. The roads here are busy: the M4 and Parramatta Road carry heavy traffic, and weekday peaks are slow. A weekend morning is far pleasanter, when the park gates open and joggers, cyclists and families spread across the grass. Fuel, food and coffee are everywhere, from the cafés in the park to the long strip of eateries in Parramatta itself.

From here you can head north-west toward the Old Great North Road, built by convicts in the 1820s and 1830s to link Sydney with the Hunter Valley, and still a magnificent piece of stonework in places, with retaining walls and culverts that have outlasted the traffic. Beyond lie the Blue Mountains, a short ride away. Summers are hot, often above thirty-five degrees, with storms in the late afternoon, and autumn is the nicest season.
t.yukkovskaya elevation@60.1,30.3:
The Karelian Isthmus, north of Saint Petersburg, was Finnish until 1940, and the place names still carry the echo: Pargolovo, Levashovo, Kuokkala, now called Repino. The Yukki Heights, or Yukkovskaya Elevation, are among the higher ground on this stretch, a ridge of sandy hills and pine forest scattered with summer houses. Many of the datchas date from the late nineteenth century, when wealthy Petersburgers began to build wooden villas with carved trim and glassed verandas among the pines.

One of the best known sits on the sea, in Repino, where the painter Ilya Repin lived from 1903 until his death in 1930. His estate, called the Penates, is now a museum, and the house, with its eccentric octagonal studio and garden, gives a sense of the artistic life of the period. Orlov's datcha belongs to the same tradition. Not far from here, the Levashovo Wasteland is the site of a memorial cemetery for victims of the repressions of the 1930s, and the pine woods hold a heavy silence.

The nearest towns, Pargolovo and Levashovo, are small, while Sertolovo, about five kilometres away, has over forty thousand people and has fuel and shops. The Priozerskoye Highway, which runs northwest toward Lake Ladoga, is the main artery, and it is busy with traffic at weekends. Quiet roads leave the highway through the villages, with sandy verges and wooden fences.

Riding here is gentle, with smooth roads and low hills. The air smells of pine resin and wood smoke, and in autumn the birch leaves fall in drifts. Mosquitoes are active in summer, and the weather can turn quickly, so keep waterproofs handy. The Gulf of Finland coast is not far, with sandy beaches and sunsets that last for hours in June. In winter the pine woods are dark and silent, and the roads can be icy.
t.the steinbok fermor s estate@60.0,30.1:
On the north shore of the Neva Bay, at the edge of the modern city, lies Lakhta, a district that was a village of Finnish and Ingrian farmers when Peter the Great first built his capital. By the nineteenth century the waterfront was dotted with country estates for the St Petersburg aristocracy, and the Steinbock-Fermor family held one of them, a park of old trees and lawns with a manor house by the Gulf of Finland. I cannot give you the details of the buildings that stand today, and the stop is better treated as a way into the area than as a single monument. The estate park, shaded and quiet, is the kind of place where the city's dacha culture began.

The coast here has changed beyond recognition. Looming over the old shoreline is the Lakhta Center, a glass tower finished in 2019 and, at about 462 metres, the tallest building in Europe. It has a twisting form, said to echo a flame or a spire, and it can be seen for miles across the flat land and water. The contrast between the low wooden villas and the huge tower is the strongest impression of the district, and the long beach below it is where the city's families go for a swim in July.

The landscape is a flat, sandy shore of pine woods, reed beds and shallow water, with the gulf freezing solid in winter and anglers drilling holes in the ice. The smell is of pine and brackish water. At midsummer the nights are never fully dark, and a stroll along the shore at eleven in the evening is possible in a pale, silver light.

Riding in Saint Petersburg is a matter of patience. Roads are wide but crowded, with trams, fast taxis and deep potholes after winter, and the surface can be hard on a motorcycle. The coastal highway is a better option for a stretch, and the ring road is useful for crossing the city. Early morning on a Sunday is calm. Fuel is easy to find, with several stations in Lakhta and Olgino, and Untolovo and the neighbouring districts have shops and cafés. Entry rules and conditions for foreign visitors can change quickly, so check before planning a trip. May to September is the best season, though the white nights of June are the high point.
t.the road of life@60.1,31.1:
On the south-eastern shore of Lake Ladoga, east of Saint Petersburg, a road ends at the water. This is the start of the Road of Life, the supply route across the ice that kept Leningrad alive during the siege of 1941 to 1944. The siege lasted 872 days, from September 1941 to January 1944, and it cut the city off from nearly everything except the lake. In the first winter, when Ladoga froze, trucks and horse-drawn sledges began to cross the ice with food and fuel, and on the return journey they carried out women, children and the sick. Lorries broke through the ice, and bombing and artillery attacked the route, but it kept going.

Memorials mark the place. A monument called the Broken Ring commemorates the breaking of the blockade, and at the lake shore a lighthouse at Osinovets and a monument known as the Flower of Life remember those who died and those who crossed. The siege is a deep wound in Russian memory, since hundreds of thousands of people died, many of them of cold and hunger, and it is treated here with real gravity. The visit is quiet and best done respectfully.

Ladoga itself is the largest lake in Europe, a grey inland sea, and the shore here is low, with reeds, pines and small beaches. The nearby town of Shlisselburg stands where the Neva leaves the lake, and its fortress, Oreshek, on an island, was founded by Novgorodians in the fourteenth century and later became a feared prison. The weather on the lake is changeable: strong winds, sudden fog and cold even in summer, and the water stays icy long after spring has arrived.

The riding is flat and straightforward, along a main road lined by forests and villages, with a fair amount of traffic near Saint Petersburg and on the road itself. In summer the light lasts late into the night, and in winter it gets dark soon after lunch, so the best time is from late May to early September. Fuel is available in Shlisselburg, Imeni Morozova and along the main road, with the large stations on the approach from the city; small villages like Borisova Griva have little. The Koltushi highway ride heads toward the village where the physiologist Ivan Pavlov built his research station, a quiet piece of science history on the way.
t.dorrigo national park@-30.4,152.8:
The Dorrigo plateau rises behind the coast of northern New South Wales like an island of rainforest in a sea of farmland, at about seven hundred metres, with rich red soil formed by ancient volcanic basalt. The national park protects the largest stand of subtropical rainforest on the plateau, and it is one of the Gondwana Rainforests sites on the World Heritage list. The trees are huge: strangler figs, brush box, tulipwood, and tree ferns in the shade beneath, with epiphytes and orchids on every branch. Walking in this forest after rain, the air smells of wet earth and leaves, and the sound of dripping is everywhere.

The best known feature is the Skywalk, a boardwalk that reaches out into the canopy and looks down over the valley toward the coast, and on a clear day the Pacific can be seen shining in the distance. Trails lead to waterfalls such as Crystal Shower Falls, where you can walk behind a curtain of water, and the cool air under the trees comes as a relief on a hot day. The wildlife is rewarding if you are patient: superb lyrebirds scratch in the leaf litter, paradise riflebirds display in the canopy, and the call of the whipbird rings out sharply.

For motorcyclists, the draw is the Waterfall Way. t.werrikimbe national park@-31.2,152.3:
Werrikimbe lies on the rim of the Great Escarpment in the hinterland of the New South Wales mid-north coast, a remote tract of high plateau, eucalypt forest and rainforest pockets, cut by deep gorges and wild rivers. t.amada@22.7,32.3:

t.australian convict sites@-33.4,151.0:

Together with other sites it is part of the UNESCO-listed Australian Convict Sites, which record the transportation of about 160,000 men, women and children from Britain.

The best-known section is at Devine's Hill, near Wisemans Ferry, where a long retaining wall holds up the road on a steep slope. Walking along it, you see the marks of tools in the stone and feel the sheer labour. Other sections, such as Finch's Line or the Convict Trail, are quieter bush tracks. This is not a place you ride to, strictly speaking. Fuel is available at Independence and Punta Gorda, though it is wise to fill the tank whenever you can in the south. The dry season, from February to May, is the best time, though also the hottest.

Pack sun cream, a hat, and a small dry bag for your gear. The water is clear and warm, and the reef begins just beyond the beach.

Peter the Great chose a swamp and told it to become a capital. The city's canals and islands, in the delta, make it feel like a northern cousin of Amsterdam or Venice.

I should be straight about riding here. Since 2022 entry into Russia for most European travellers has been very difficult, with restricted land borders, sanctions, and restrictions on insurance and vehicle documents, and the situation changes frequently. If you are reading this as a plan, check the current rules first. As a place, though, the Neva is among the great rivers of European history.

If you do get there, the roads within the city are wide, with heavy traffic, trams, and tricky bridges, and the cobbles and tram rails are slippery in the wet. Petrol stations are plentiful around the ring road and on the main routes, and the suburbs along the river have all the usual services. The weather is cool and damp for much of the year, with winters that are dark and icy, and the best months are June to August.

t.springfield illinois@39.8,-89.7:

t.meriwether lewis site@35.5,-87.5:
Here the Natchez Trace Parkway comes to a monument that carries a story with a question mark at the end. In October 1809, Meriwether Lewis, famed for the expedition to the Pacific with William Clark, stopped at a roadside inn called Grinder's Stand while travelling to Washington, and in the early hours of the next morning he was found dead of gunshot wounds. A tall broken column, raised in 1848, marks his grave, and it is a sober, quiet place in the middle of the trees.

A short section of the original trail is preserved here, a sunken path under the trees, along with the foundations of the inn and a small cabin. The surface is excellent, the corners are easy and the scenery shifts slowly from hardwood forest to farmland. Deer are the hazard, especially at dawn and dusk, and it pays to watch the verges. Lawrenceburg, a town of some ten thousand people about thirty kilometres south, has the services you need, and Hohenwald is closer to the north. t.hohenwald@35.5,-87.6:

t.berowra old road@-33.6,151.2:

Berowra has around four and a half thousand people and Berowra Heights, next door, a little more, so fuel, bakeries, cafes and a station are close at hand. t.bellingen@-30.5,152.9:

t.ebor falls@-30.4,152.4:

t.kurrajong heights@-33.5,150.6:

A hot pie and a coffee from a village bakery is the traditional first stop for a ride heading out toward the mountains. t.mount tomah@-33.5,150.4:
Mount Tomah is the high point on the Bells Line of Road, at about a thousand metres, and it is capped with basalt, which makes all the difference. While the surrounding Blue Mountains are made of sandstone with thin, poor soil, the volcanic cap here has rich, deep earth that holds water and grows big trees, rhododendrons, camellias and cold-climate plants that would never survive on the coast. The surface is mostly good, but the cold can bring frost in winter, and fog sits on the ridge in the mornings. Because of the elevation, thunderstorms can sweep in quickly in the afternoon.

The forests around Mount Tomah are home to wombats, wallabies, lyrebirds and more cockatoos than you can count. At dusk, animals come out onto the verges, so keep your speed down once the light goes. The Wollemi National Park, a vast sandstone wilderness with few roads, lies north of the road, and the Grose Valley is to the south, so the road follows a spine between two enormous areas of protected country.

For fuel, do not rely on the garden. Blackheath, about sixteen kilometres to the west, is the closest sizeable stop, and Richmond lies down the hill to the east. Wentworth Falls is larger still. t.colo river@-33.4,150.8:
The Colo River is the wild neighbour of the Hawkesbury. It rises in the rugged sandstone country of Wollemi National Park, one of the largest wilderness areas in New South Wales, and it runs through gorges that no road has ever reached before joining the Hawkesbury near the point where the valley opens out. The river is a cool place to take a break in summer, and a pull-off near the bridge gives access to the water for a paddle. Be careful with swimming, because the currents can be stronger than they look. Canoeists and kayakers use the river, and there are camping spots along the banks, though you should check which are open and whether permits are required. In the hot, dry months, bushfire danger can be extreme, and roads may close, so follow the local alerts.

East Kurrajong, about nine kilometres away, is small, and Richmond, about twenty kilometres, is the safest place to fill before the long run north. The Putty Road itself has very few services over its length, so a full tank is essential.
t.halfway house@-33.1,150.7:
